Sūrat al-Najm (Sura of the Star)

It is also called Sūrat al-Najm without the waw. It is Meccan without qualification. In al-Itqan (al-Suyuti's Al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an), an exception is made from it: ﴿Those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾ up to ﴿and He is the one who gives satisfaction﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. It is said that the exception is ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away﴾ [al-Najm: 33] through the nine verses. It is a strange report that al-Tabarsi transmits from al-Hasan that it is Medinan. I see no soundness in that attribution from him at all. Its verses number sixty-two according to the Kufan count, and sixty-one according to other counts. It is, as Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, the first surah in which the Prophet (ﷺ) publicly recited, and he recited it in the Sacred Precinct while the polytheists were listening.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from him (Ibn Mas'ud) who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was 'al-Najm'. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and all the people prostrated with him except a man whom I saw take a handful of dirt and prostrate upon it. I later saw him killed as a disbeliever." He was Umayyah ibn Khalaf. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is reported: "He (peace be upon him) prostrated, and the believers, the polytheists, the jinn and the humans prostrated with him, except Abu Lahab, who raised a handful of dirt and said, 'This suffices.'" It is possible that he and Umayyah both did the same thing.

It is strongly connected to what precedes it, for al-Tur ended with His saying, ﴿and after the setting of the stars﴾ [al-Tur: 49], and this surah begins with His saying, ﴿By the star﴾. Also, its opening contains what affirms the refutation of the disbelievers' accusations against him (ﷺ) of fabricating speech, poetry, soothsaying and madness. Abu Hayyan mentions that the occasion of its revelation was the statement of the polytheists that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was fabricating the Qur'an. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned, regarding its connection to al-Tur, that al-Tur contains mention of the offspring of the believers and that they follow their fathers, while this surah contains mention of the offspring of the Jews in His saying, ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the bellies of your mothers﴾ [al-Najm: 32], and so on.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabari, Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah and al-Wahidi narrated from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, when a small child of theirs died, would say, 'He is a righteous one (siddiq).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said, 'The Jews have lied. No soul that Allah creates in its mother's belly is anything but either wretched or blessed.' Then Allah revealed at that point, ﴿He knows you best﴾, the whole verse." And when He, exalted is He, said there regarding the believers, ﴿We shall unite them with their offspring﴾ [al-Tur: 21], etc., He, glorified is He, said here regarding the disbelievers, or regarding adults, ﴿and that man has nothing but what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], contrary to what was included regarding the believing children. Then he said: This is a wondrous aspect of connection, from the category of opposition. However, regarding the soundness of His saying, ﴿He knows you best﴾, that it was revealed when the matter was mentioned, I have reservations; and that His saying, ﴿We shall unite them with their offspring﴾, refers to children, is not agreed upon by the commentators, as you have heard, which is not far-fetched. Indeed, whoever reflects will find aspects of connection other than what was mentioned, so reflect.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the star when it sets﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swears by the genus of the well-known star, according to what is narrated from al-Hasan and Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, and from it is the poet's saying:

So she spent the night counting the stars, in a hiding place, quick with the hands of those who eat, their dried-up flesh.

The meaning of (hawa) is "set" (gharaba). It is said also that it means "rose" (tala'a). One says hawa yahwi, like rama yarmi, hawyan with a fatha, in the sense of falling and setting, because of its resemblance to that; and huwiyyan with a damma, for ascending and rising. It is said also that hawa with a fatha is for ascending and hawa with a damma is for descending. It is said that hawa with fatha and damma both mean falling. One also says ahwa in the sense of hawa. Some lexicographers distinguished between them, saying that hawa is when something swoops down without a prey, and ahwa is when it swoops down for one.

when it swoops down for it. Al-Hasan and Abu Hamza al-Thumali said: He swears, glorified is He, by the stars when they scatter on the Day of Resurrection. From Ibn Abbas, in one narration, He swears, mighty and majestic is He, by the stars when they are cast in pursuit of the devils. It is said that the star refers to a specific one. Mujahid and Sufyan said: it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), since "the star" became a proper designation for it by dominance. From this is his (ﷺ) saying: "When the star rises in the morning, blight is lifted." And the Arabs' saying: "The star rose in the evening, so the herdsman sought a cloak; the star rose at morning, so the herdsman sought a... (kasiyyah)." Its setting was explained as its falling with the dawn. It is said that it is Sirius (al-Shi'ra), which is meant by His saying, ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾ [al-Najm: 49], and the soothsayers used to speak of unseen matters at its rising. It is said that it is Venus, which was worshipped. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Farra' and Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: (the star) is the measure of the Qur'an that descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and (when it sets) means when it descended upon him together with the angel of revelation, Jibril (peace be upon him). Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the Prophet (ﷺ), and his setting is his descent from the sky on the night of the Mi'raj. It is permissible on this view that his setting means his ascent and elevation (peace and blessings be upon him) to the furthest limit. It is said that it is the scholars, taking it as a genus, and their setting is said to be their ascent in the stations of success to the enclosures of realization. It is said also that it is their diving into the seas of thought to extract the pearls of secrets. The most apparent of the views is that the star refers to the genus of the well-known star, since its origin is a generic noun for every heavenly body; and according to the view of a specific one, the most apparent is that it is the Pleiades. Beyond these two views is the view that it refers to the measure of the Qur'an that descended. In swearing by this, to affirm his (peace be upon him) freedom from any trace of error and misguidance, there is an astonishing eloquence and beauty of placement with no limit beyond it. As for the first views, it is because the star's characteristic is that the traveller is guided by it to the paths of the world, as if it were said: "By the star by which the wayfarers are guided to the right way."

**"Your companion has not gone astray"** (﴿ما ضَلَّ صاحِبُكُمْ﴾): that is, he has not deviated from the path of truth, which is the way to the Hereafter. This is a metaphor (istiʿara) and an allegorical image (tamthil) for the fact that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was right in his sayings and his deeds. **"Nor has he erred"** (﴿وما غَوى﴾): that is, he never held a false belief at all, because *al-ghayy* is ignorance accompanied by corrupt belief, and it is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). Therefore the coordination of this clause with "has not gone astray" is an instance of mentioning the specific after the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm), out of concern for belief and as an indication that it is the pivot of the matter.

As for the third view, it is an honouring of the Qur'an's status and an alert to the basis of his guidance, peace and blessings be upon him, and the foundation of his rectitude. It is as if it were said: "And what was sent down to you of the Qur'an, which is knowledge in guidance to the methods of the religion and the paths of truth and certainty, [your companion] Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, has not gone astray from it, nor has he erred." This is from the same type as the line of poetry: *wa-thanayāka innahā iġrīḍ* ("and your front teeth, for indeed they are freshly opened white blossoms"). The address is to the Quraysh, and the mention of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, by the designation of "companion" (*al-musāhaba*) is to signal that they were aware of the detailed circumstances of his noble life and had full knowledge of his freedom from everything denied of him absolutely, and of his being characterized, peace and blessings be upon him, by the utmost guidance and rectitude. For the long companionship they had with him, peace and blessings be upon him, and their witnessing of the noble excellences of his great affairs necessarily entail this. Thus there is in this a confirmation of establishing the proof against them.

Scholars differed concerning the complement of *idhā* (when) in God's words: **"By the star when it sets"** (﴿والنَّجْمِ إذا هَوى﴾). Someone said: I debated Jar Allah (al-Zamakhshari) on His words, and he said: "The governing element (*al-ʿāmil*) in it is what the *wāw* (of the oath) is attached to." I said: "How can the verb of the present (*fiʿl al-ḥāl*) govern in the future?" This is because its meaning is "I swear now, I do not swear after this." He then reversed himself and said: "The governing element in it is a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar maḥdhūf), and the estimate is: 'and the star fell when it fell.'" I presented this to some of the shaykhs, and his second statement was not approved. The correct view is that it is attached to *aqsama* (I swear), and the sense of futurity has been stripped from it, so that it becomes for bare time, like your saying, "I will come to you when the dates ripen" (*ātīka idhā iḥmarra al-busr*), meaning at the time of its reddening.

ʿAbd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) said: God's announcement of what is expected (*al-mutawaqqaʿ*) is treated as the announcement of what has occurred, since there is no doubt about it; so the future takes the place of the realized past. It has also been said that it is attached to a governing element which is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the star." It was objected to this that time cannot be a predicate or a circumstantial clause for a solid entity (*juththa*) as here, and that *idhā* is for the future, so how can it be a circumstantial clause, except if it is a clause of anticipated state (ḥāl muqaddara), or if the bare *idhā* is for unrestricted time, as it is said that the circumstantial function is valid when it conveys a meaningful sense. So the occurrence of time as a predicate or circumstantial clause for a solid entity is not absolutely forbidden, as the grammarians stated. Or [it may refer to] the star, since its change in rising and setting resembles an event (*ḥadath*). Fairness dictates that making it a circumstantial clause, like attaching it to a deleted verbal noun, is not the correct view. The correct view, as has been said, is what I heard about its attachment to *aqsama*, with the sense of futurity stripped from it; and this is what the author of *al-Mughni* (Ibn Hisham, *Mughni al-Labib*) chose. The specification of the oath to the time of the star's descent is evident according to the last of the three views. As for the first two views, it has been said: because the star does not serve as a guide for the traveller when it is at the middle of the sky, nor does it show the east from the west or the north from the south; it is only used for guidance when it descends or ascends. Along with this there is a complete suitability to what will be related of its falling and approaching. It has also been said: because of its indication of its having come into being, which indicates the Creator and the greatness of His power, glory be to Him, as the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham), upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of blessings and the most perfect of peace, said: **"I do not love those that set"** (﴿لا أُحِبُّ الآفِلِينَ﴾) [al-Anʿam: 76].

The complete discussion of the detailed grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of such a construction will come, God willing, at the end of the book, so do not be negligent.

﴿And he does not speak﴾, i.e., the Prophet (ﷺ), since his mention preceded in His saying: ﴿your companion﴾. Speech (النُّطْقُ, al-nutq) is taken to include the meaning of issuing forth (الصُّدُورُ, al-sudur), and therefore it is followed by عَنِ ("from") in His saying: ﴿from desire﴾. It has been said that عَنِ here has the meaning of بِ ("by" or "with"), but this is not the case. That is, his utterance does not issue forth regarding what he has brought you from Him, Mighty and Majestic, such as the Qur'an, or from the Qur'an, out of the desire of his own self or his opinion at all. For the intended meaning is the continuity of the negation, as has passed many times in its like.

﴿It is not﴾, meaning: what is it that he utters of that or of the Qur'an? All of this is understood from the context. ﴿but a revelation﴾ from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿revealed﴾, which He, glorified be He, reveals to him. The clause is a descriptive clause confirming "revelation," removing the possibility of metaphor and indicating continuous renewal. It has also been said that the pronoun in "he utters" refers to the Qur'an, so the verse is like His saying, ﴿This, Our Book, speaks against you with truth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], though this is contrary to the apparent meaning. It has also been said that what is meant is that what issues from his utterance, peace and blessings be upon him, is absolutely free from desire, and this refers to whatever he utters in general.

Those who did not regard ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) as permissible for him, peace and blessings be upon him, such as Abu Ali al-Jubba'i and his son Abu Hashim, used this verse to support this interpretation. The basis of their argument is that Allah, Most High, informed that everything he utters is revelation, and what derives from ijtihad is not revelation, so it is not among what he utters. It is answered that when Allah permits him, peace and blessings be upon him, to perform ijtihad, then ijtihad and what is attributed to it become revelation, not speech from desire. Its essence is a denial of the major premise of analogy (qiyas). It is objected that this would entail that the rulings which the mujtahids (jurists who perform ijtihad) derive by analogy are revelation. It is answered that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was revealed to perform ijtihad, unlike other mujtahids. Al-Qadi al-Baydawi said: "In that case it is by revelation, not revelation itself." Sahib al-Kashf responded that this is not a valid objection, because it is equivalent to Allah, Most High, saying to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whenever you think of such a thing, it is My ruling," meaning: "Whatever I cast into your heart is what I intend," so it is revelation in reality. The apparent meaning is that the verse was revealed concerning the matter of the Revelation (al-Tanzil) specifically, although sacred hadiths (al-ahadith al-qudsiyyah, sayings in which the meaning is from Allah while the wording is the Prophet's) are similar to it. Using it to prove that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was not bound to revelation requires departing from the apparent meaning and straining to repel al-Baydawi's objection, may Allah have mercy on him, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

In my view, it is not far-fetched that His saying, ﴿nor does he speak from desire﴾, be understood in its general sense. Those who hold that ijtihad is permissible for him, peace and blessings be upon him, such as Imam Ahmad and Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on them both,
[p. 47]
do not say that what he utters, peace and blessings be upon him, of what his ijtihad has led him to, proceeds from the desire of the soul and its appetite. Far be the presence of the Message from that. Rather, they say that it is an intermediary between that and revelation. The pronoun in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿It is not but a revelation﴾ is taken to refer to the Qur'an, on the basis that the statement is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "If his condition, peace and blessings be upon him, is that he does not speak from desire, then what is this Qur'an which he brought, which opposed what his people held, which won over the hearts of many people, and about which many sayings have multiplied?" It is said: "It is nothing but a revelation which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, reveals to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. So reflect."

In al-Kashf it is said that His saying, Most High, ﴿what he utters﴾ in the present tense, together with His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾, indicates that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had no past of error or deviation since he was distinguished (from others), and before his maturing and his being made a prophet he had no speech from desire. How could he, when he was matured and made a prophet? In this there is an exhortation to them to witness his wise speech.

[﴿He taught him﴾] The pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the second object (*maf'ūl thānī*, the second direct object) is omitted, meaning the Qur'an or the revelation. Abū Ḥayyān permitted that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and that the first object (*maf'ūl awwal*) is omitted, meaning: the Messenger, peace be upon him, taught it. ﴿One mighty in power﴾ is Jibrīl (Gabriel), peace be upon him, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ, for he is the intermediary in the manifestation of the extraordinary events. A sufficient proof of the intensity of his strength is that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lūṭ (Lot) from the black water beneath the earth, carried them on his wing, lifted them up to the heaven, then overturned them. He also cried out at Thamūd with a single shout, so they became lifeless bodies lying prostrate. His descent to the prophets, peace be upon them, and his ascent were faster than the blink of an eye. By my life, he is faster than the movement of the sunlight, according to what they have established in the so-called *al-Ḥikmah al-Jadīdah* (the "New Philosophy").

**﴿Possessor of strength﴾**: one of sound judgment and firm intellect, as some have said. So the first (Gabriel's description in the preceding verse) was described by the strength of his action, and this one (Gabriel's description here) by the strength of his insight and intellect. It has been said, however, that this is an explanation of what the word was coined for, since the Arabs say of one who has strong intellect and judgment that he is *dhū mirra* (possessor of strength), from *umrirat al-ḥabl* (the rope was made firm) when its twisting has been tightened. Otherwise, describing an angel with such a quality is not evident. Thus it is a metaphor for the manifestation of wondrous effects.

From Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: "one of wisdom," because the speech of the wise is firm. Al-Tastī (al-Ṭasṭī) narrated that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about it, and he said: "One of strength in the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic," and he cited evidence for it. Al-Ṭībī (al-Ṭībī) related from him that he said: "One of fine appearance," and al-Ṭabarī (al-Ṭabarī) approved of this. In the same sense is the saying of Mujahid: "One of good character." This is in his (ﷺ) saying: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who is *dhū mirra* (possessing strength) and sound," meaning *dhū quwwa* (possessing power). In al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshāf) it is said that *al-mirra* in origin indicates "once after once," which indicates an increase in strength, so do not overlook this.

**﴿Then he stood firm﴾**: that is, he stood upright in his true form upon which Allah created him. This was at Ḥirā' at the beginning of prophethood, and the Messenger (ﷺ) had with him—as in a hadith narrated by Imam Aḥmad, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, and a group, from Ibn Mas'ud—six hundred wings, each wing of which fills the horizon. So *al-istiwā'* (standing firm) here means the balance (i'tidāl) of a thing in its essence, as al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said, and this is what is meant by *al-istiqāma* (uprightness), not the opposite of crookedness. From this comes *istawā al-thamar* (the fruit became ripe) when it matured.

In the speech of al-Khafājī (al-Khafājī), as he said: there is a folding, because describing him (peace be upon him) with strength and some human attributes indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him in other than his true form. This is an elaboration in answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "Did he see him in his true form?" So it is said: "Yes, he saw him, and stood firm..." etc.

In al-Irshād (Irshād al-'Aql al-Salīm) it is said that it is a conjunction with "his teaching him" by way of explanation, since from His saying "what He revealed" onward is an explanation of the manner of teaching. It has been criticized that the manner is not restricted to what has been mentioned. From here it has been said that the *fā'* (then) is for causation, since his (peace be upon him) taking on a human form is caused by his power and ability over extraordinary matters; or that it is conjunctive to "taught him," in the sense: "he taught him in other than his original form, then stood firm in his original form." It has been criticized that the arrangement of speech is not complete with this and the order is not made fine by it.

It has also been said:

*istawā* means "rose up," and the conjunction is to "taught," meaning: he rose to the heaven after he had taught him. Most of the transmitted reports, however, require what has preceded.

﴿And he was on the highest horizon﴾. That is, the highest direction of the sky, facing the observer. Its original meaning is "the region" (al-nāḥiyah). What the people of the hay'ah (astronomy, the science of celestial configuration) mention is a technical meaning (iṣṭilāḥī), and it is divided in their usage into a true (ḥaqīqī) horizon and others, as explained in its proper place. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that what is meant here is the rising point of the sun. Its meaning is also the statement of al-Ḥasan: "It is the horizon of the east."

The clause is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject) from the subject of istawā (he rose level).

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī said: "Wa-huwa" is a ʿaṭf (conjunction) upon the hidden pronoun in istawā, and that pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), just as that [pronoun] refers to Jibrīl (peace be upon him). The reverse was also permitted. The prepositional phrase (bi-l-ufuq) is connected to istawā, and in this there is ʿaṭf upon the raised pronoun without a separating element (faṣl), which is the position of the Kufans, although the meaning does not follow it according to the majority.

﴿Then he drew near﴾, meaning: then Gabriel, peace be upon him, drew near to the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿And hung suspended﴾, meaning: Gabriel, peace and blessings be upon him, was suspended in the air. From this comes the expression "the fruit hung down" (tadallat al-thamarah), and he "let down his legs from the bed" (dalla rijlayhi min al-sarir). Al-dawali means fruit hanging down like bunches of grapes. They recited, citing Abu Dhu'ayb, describing one who gathers honey:

*He hung down over them between a cliff's edge and a rope, on a bare rock like a drop, sliding down.*

From the rhymed sayings of Ibnat al-Khass: "Be wary, like the *qirilla* (a small bird): if it sees good, it swoops down (tadallá); if it sees evil, it turns away (tawallá)." So the meaning of *tadalli* is a specific kind of nearness, and there is no need for inversion (qalb) or for interpreting it as "nearness" as in al-Idah. Yet if it is taken to mean "descending from a height," as the derivation (ishtiqaq) suggests, then it has a basis.

﴿And was﴾, meaning: Gabriel, peace be upon him, was from the Prophet (ﷺ) ﴿at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾, meaning: of the bows of the Arabs, because unrestricted usage is understood according to their customary usage. *Al-qab*, as well as *al-qayb*, *al-qad* and *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* (measure), are all terms for measure. Zayd ibn Ali read *qad*, and *qayd* and *qadr* are also recited. Measurement by the bow has been attested, as with the spear and the forearm, and others. It is said to refer to the distance between the grip of the bow and its string, which is what is bent at its two ends, so each bow has two *qab*s. Some explained it this way here. It was said: there is inversion (qalb) in the expression, meaning "the two qab-ends of a bow." Al-Kashf says you may say *qaban qawsin* and *qab qawsayn* as one unit without inversion. It is also reported from Mujahid and al-Hasan that *qab al-qaws* is the distance between its string and its grip, and there is no need for inversion here either. This, according to what al-Khafaji said, refers to what the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to do when they made alliances: they would bring out two bows and stick one to the other, so that the *qab* of one touched the other, as though they were a single *qab*. Then they would draw them together and shoot one arrow with them. This signified that one's consent is the other's consent, and one's anger is the other's anger, and it is impossible to oppose it.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that *al-qaws* here is a forearm by which lengths are measured, and Abu Razin adopted this view. Al-Tha'labi mentioned that it is from the dialect of the Hijaz. Whatever the case, the meaning depends on the omission of an annexed noun (mudaf), that is: "one having the measure of two bow-lengths," and similar to it is the line of verse:

*When its limping overtook the retreating locust, and it had made me as far as Khuzaymah's finger.*

This means "having the measure of one finger," and it denotes nearness. So it is as if it was said: "and was near to him." It is also permitted that the pronoun in *kana* refers to the distance, interpreted as "remoteness" or similar, so there is no need to posit an omission, though this is not the best view.

﴿Or nearer﴾, meaning: or closer than that. ("Or," *aw*, here expresses uncertainty from the viewpoint of the servants, in the sense that when the observer saw him he would say: "He was two bow-lengths away, or nearer.") The purpose is to convey the extreme degree of nearness.

﴿And was﴾, meaning: Gabriel, peace be upon him, was from the Prophet (ﷺ) ﴿at a distance of two bow-lengths﴾, meaning: of the bows of the Arabs, because unrestricted usage is understood according to their customary usage. *Al-qab*, as well as *al-qayb*, *al-qad* and *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* (measure), are all terms for measure. Zayd ibn Ali read *qad*, and *qayd* and *qadr* are also recited. Measurement by the bow has been attested, as with the spear and the forearm, and others. It is said to refer to the distance between the grip of the bow and its string, which is what is bent at its two ends, so each bow has two *qab*s. Some explained it this way here. It was said: there is inversion (qalb) in the expression, meaning "the two qab-ends of a bow." Al-Kashf says you may say *qaban qawsin* and *qab qawsayn* as one unit without inversion. It is also reported from Mujahid and al-Hasan that *qab al-qaws* is the distance between its string and its grip, and there is no need for inversion here either. This, according to what al-Khafaji said, refers to what the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to do when they made alliances: they would bring out two bows and stick one to the other, so that the *qab* of one touched the other, as though they were a single *qab*. Then they would draw them together and shoot one arrow with them. This signified that one's consent is the other's consent, and one's anger is the other's anger, and it is impossible to oppose it.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that *al-qaws* here is a forearm by which lengths are measured, and Abu Razin adopted this view. Al-Tha'labi mentioned that it is from the dialect of the Hijaz. Whatever the case, the meaning depends on the omission of an annexed noun (mudaf), that is: "one having the measure of two bow-lengths," and similar to it is the line of verse:

*When its limping overtook the retreating locust, and it had made me as far as Khuzaymah's finger.*

This means "having the measure of one finger," and it denotes nearness. So it is as if it was said: "and was near to him." It is also permitted that the pronoun in *kana* refers to the distance, interpreted as "remoteness" or similar, so there is no need to posit an omission, though this is not the best view.

﴿Or nearer﴾, meaning: or closer than that. ("Or," *aw*, here expresses uncertainty from the viewpoint of the servants, in the sense that when the observer saw him he would say: "He was two bow-lengths away, or nearer.") The purpose is to convey the extreme degree of nearness.

﴿Then He revealed﴾, i.e., Jibril, peace be upon him, ﴿to His servant﴾, i.e., the servant of Allah, who is the Prophet (ﷺ). The use of the pronoun (al-idmar) without a prior mention of Allah is because He is in the utmost clarity. Many examples of this occur in speech, and among them is ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for what they have earned, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single creature﴾ [Fatir: 45].

[Page 49]

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. ﴿What He revealed﴾, i.e., that which He revealed, and the concealed pronoun is also for Jibril, peace be upon him. The vagueness regarding what was revealed is for magnification. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Taha: 78]. Abu Zayd said: the concealed pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, i.e., Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah what Allah had revealed to Jibril. The first [view] is narrated from al-Hasan and is the best. It was also said: the pronoun in (awha) the first and the second both refer to Allah, Exalted, and the intended "servant" is Jibril, peace be upon him, and this, as you see, [is weak].

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ That is, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what he saw with his eyes of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, what his heart (ﷺ) said when it saw him with his eyes was not "I do not recognize you." Had it said that, it would have been lying, because it recognized him with the heart just as it saw him with the eyes. So it comes from their saying "kadhib" when one speaks a lie, and "ma kadhaba" means "ma qala al-kadhib" (did not speak a lie). It was also said that the meaning is: the eye did not lie to the heart in what it conveyed to it of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). Things in the realm of the malakut (the unseen, spiritual dominion) are perceived first by the heart and then pass from it to the eye.

Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Khalid ibn Ilyas and Hisham, on the authority of Ibn Amir, read ﴿ما كَذَّبَ﴾ with a shaddah, meaning that it did not deny its truth and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form. The verses contain what they contain of establishing the reality of revelation. In al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), it says: when He, glorified is He, said ﴿It is nothing but a revelation that is revealed﴾, meaning from Allah, the Exalted, He mentioned what depicts this meaning and details it, so that it would be confirmed that it is revelation and that it is in no way from poetry or the talk of soothsayers (kahin). So He said: your companion knew this revelation, who it is with these attributes. His saying, ﴿So he stood firm﴾, and the narration of his standing in his true form, is to affirm that what came to him in the form of Dihya is the same being. He saw him in his own form and knew him as he truly is, so nothing about him can be confused for anything else. His saying, ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾, completes the account of his descent to him (peace be upon him) and his coming to him in the dwelling. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Then He revealed﴾, means that Jibril revealed that revelation, which has passed, that it is from Allah, the Exalted, to the servant of Allah. He said, glorified is He, "what He revealed," and did not use a pronoun, to magnify the status of the One who sent it down, and that it is something beyond description. So how could anyone presume to say it is poetry or the talk of a soothsayer? Choosing "His servant" as the object, instead of "to him," that is, to your companion, is for the sake of the idafa of exclusivity. Using the pronoun rather than the proper name in this position is to make it the more fitting (tarshih), and because he is a servant only of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, there is no ambiguity, since he is famous as the servant of Allah and nothing else. It is also possible that the sense is: then Allah, the Exalted, revealed through his agency, that is, through the agency of this teacher, to His servant. The fa' in "fa-awha" indicates this meaning, and this too is a sound view. Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, meaning that once it recognized him and verified him, his heart did not deny him afterwards, even if he appeared in a form other than that one, saying he is Jibril. This is a secret and carefully observed composition, containing subtleties given their full due, consistent with reality, and it does not depart from the obligatory harmony between the beginning and the end. End of quotation.

This is a precious statement, by which he gives preference to what is narrated from A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her). That will come, Allah willing, with what is for it and against it.

Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, on surah 53, verse 12:

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ That is: Will you deny him and then argue with him about what he sees with his own eyes? "Fatumarunahu" (will you dispute with him) is coordinated with a elided element, according to al-Zamakhshari's view of *mira'* (disputation), which means *mujadalah* (argumentation). Its derivation is from *maraytu al-naqah* (I stroked the she-camel), when one strokes her back and udder so that her milk comes out and flows. Argument was likened to this, because each of the two disputants seeks to learn what the other has, so that the other is bound by the proof; it is as if he is extracting its milk.

Ali, may God ennoble his face, and Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, al-Jahdari, Ya'qub, Ibn Sa'dan, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *"afatumrunahu"* with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and a *sukun* on the *mim*, as the imperfect of *maraytu*, meaning *jahadtu* (I denied). It is said: *maraytuhu haqqahu* (I denied him his right) when I denied it to him. They cited for this the verse of the poet:

*"If you forsake a brother of truthfulness and nobility, you have indeed denied a brother who would never deny you."*

[Page 50]

Or it is the imperfect of *maraytuhu*, when I overcame him in *mira'*, so that it belongs to the category of *mughalabah* (overpowering). The verse may be read in this sense as well. The verb is construed with *ʿala* (on), whereas its original construction would be with *fi* (in), because it is taken to imply the meaning of overpowering, since both the disputant and the denier intend by their action to overcome the opponent.

Abdullah, as related by Ibn Khalawayh, and al-Sha'bi, as mentioned by Shu'bah, read *"afatumrunahu"* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *sukun* on the *mim*, as the imperfect of *amraytu*. Abu Hatim said: "This is an error."

What is meant by *ma yara* (what he sees) is what he saw of the form of Jibril, peace be upon him. The imperfect is used to bring the past appearance vividly to mind because of its strangeness. In al-Bahr it is said: the imperfect form is used, although the seeing had already occurred, to indicate what may still happen afterwards. It is also said that what is meant by *"Will you then dispute with him about what he sees"* is the forms in which Jibril, peace be upon him, appears after he had seen him before and had verified him, such that no matter in what form he appeared, he would not be confused about him. In this case the use of the imperfect remains on its apparent sense.

﴿And he certainly saw him﴾, that is, the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Jibril (Gabriel) in the form in which Allah created him, ﴿another descent﴾, that is, another time of descending. It is a form (*fi'la*) of *nuzul* (descent) placed in the position of *marra* (an occurrence). Its accusative case is *naṣb al-ẓarfiyya* (adverbial accusative of time), because the root of *marra* is the verbal noun of *marra, yamurru*, and because the verb is so closely tied to time, it is expressed by it. He did not say *marratan* instead, in order to convey that the seeing on this occasion was with descent and approach, like the seeing on the first occasion, which is indicated by what has already passed.

Al-Ḥawfī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *nazlatan* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl muqaddara*), meaning "descending a descent." Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted it to be in the accusative as a verbal noun of *ra'ā* (to see) derived from its meaning, that is, "another seeing," but there is a point of concern regarding this.

The purpose of the oath clause is to negate doubt and suspicion regarding the last occasion, and that occasion was the Night of the Isrāʾ (Night Journey).

﴿Ḥindahū ʿinda sidrat al-muntahā﴾ ("near the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary"). It is, according to the well-known view, a jujube (*nabq*) tree to the right of the Throne in the seventh heaven. There is a hadith, related by Aḥmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhī and others, which says: "In the sixth heaven, its jujube fruits are like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. A rider passes in its shade for seventy years without crossing it." Al-Ḥākim related it and graded it authentic, from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "A rider would travel among its branches for a hundred years." These hadiths clearly indicate that it is a real jujube tree.

Plant life in the observable world grows from earth, water and air, and it is not far from Allah, exalted is He, to create it in whatever place He wills. He, glorified is He, has informed us that the tree of *zaqqūm* grows at the root of Hellfire. It has also been said that calling it a *sidra* is figurative (*majāz*), because the angels, peace be upon them, gather around it just as people gather in the shade of a lote-tree.

*Al-muntahā* (المُنْتَهى) is a noun of place, and it has been permitted that it be a noun of time or a *mīmī* verbal noun. It has also been said that it is called "the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary" because, as ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, the knowledge of every scholar ends at it, and what lies beyond it no one knows except Allah, exalted is He. Or because the knowledge of the prophets, peace be upon them, ends at it, and their knowledge falls short of what is beyond it. Or because the deeds of creation end at it, so that they are presented to Allah, exalted is He, there. Or because what descends from above it and what ascends from below it ends at it. Or because the spirits of the martyrs, or the spirits of believers in general, end at it. Or because of the arrival of the one who is raised up to it in honour. In *al-Kashshāf* it is said: "It is as if it were the boundary and the last point of Paradise."

The *iḍāfa* (annexation) of *sidra* to *al-muntahā* is an annexation of a thing to its location, as in "the trees of the garden." It has also been permitted that it be an annexation of a location to its attribute, as in your saying *kitāb al-fiqh* ("the book of jurisprudence"). It has also been said that *al-muntahā* may refer to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, so that the annexation is of ownership to the owner, meaning "the lote-tree of Allah, to whom is the utmost boundary," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 42]. This is to be counted as a case of ellipsis and attribution (*min bāb al-ḥadhf wa al-īṣāl*). It is not hidden that this view almost reaches the furthest extreme of remoteness.

﴿Near it﴾, meaning near the Lote-tree (al-Sidrah). It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the descent (al-nazlah), and it is then descending from the rank of acceptance. ﴿the Garden of Refuge﴾, which the righteous (al-muttaqun) will take as their refuge on the Day of Resurrection, as narrated from al-Hasan. From this it has been inferred that the Garden is in the heavens. Ibn 'Abbas, in a report that differs from him, and Qatadah said: it is a garden to which the souls of the martyrs (al-shuhada') retreat, and it is not the one promised to the righteous. It was also said: it is a garden to which the angels (peace be upon them) retreat. The first view is the most apparent. The word al-ma'wa, as the majority have stated explicitly, is a noun of place (ism makan), and the idafah of "Garden" to it is explanatory (bayaniyyah). It was also said that it is an idafah of a modified noun to its qualifier, as in masjid al-jami' (the congregational mosque). This was objected to on the grounds that a noun of place is not described by it. The clause is circumstantial (hal). It was also said that the circumstantial element is the adverbial phrase (zarf), and "Garden" (jannatu) is raised by it as its agent (fa'iliyyah).

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Ibn al-Zubayr, Anas, Zirr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Qatadah read: "jinnahu" with the pronoun attached, the pronoun referring to the Prophet (ﷺ). Junna is a verb in the past tense, meaning: "near it, its covering (sitruhu)," that is, Allah's sheltering (iwa') of him and His gracious handling of him. Or: "the refuge covered him with its shade." It is included under the view that al-ma'wa is a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi) or a noun of place, and janna-hu means "sitarahu" (covered him). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is anomalous (shadh), and the commonly used form is ajannahu. For this reason 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said, and likewise the Companions, may Allah's pleasure be upon them all, gathered: "Whoever reads it thus, Allah has made him a madman (fa-ajannahu Allah), that is, made him insane, or caused him to enter the janan, which is the grave." You know that if it is established that the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, and those with him among the senior Companions, read it this way, then no one has the right to reject it on the basis of irregularity in usage. And 'A'ishah has also been reported to have permitted it.

(Verse 16) ﴿When there covered the lote-tree that which covered it.﴾ The phrase إذْ يَغْشى السِّدْرَةَ ما يَغْشى is connected to رَآهُ (ra'ahu, "he saw him"). It was also said that it is connected to what comes after the negated clause, and placing it before the negating particle ما (ma) is not harmful, since this is for the sake of expanding the adverbial phrase (tawassu' fi al-zarf).

Al-ghashayan (the covering) means concealing and veiling, and from it comes al-ghawashi (the overshadowing things). It may also mean coming, as one says: fulan yaghsha Zaydan kull hin, meaning he comes to him at all times. The first meaning is the more fitting to the context. In leaving unspecified what (yaghsha) it is that covers, there is a glorification that is not hidden: the one covering is a matter that the scope of expression cannot encompass and the sleeves of minds cannot contain. The use of the present tense (al-mudari') is to narrate a past situation, to bring its wondrous image vividly before the mind. It is also permitted that it indicates the continuation of the covering in a renewed manner.

Some reports specify this coverer. From al-Hasan: the Light of the Lord of Might (jalla sha'nuhu) covered it, and so it was illuminated. Similar to this is what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah: the light of the Creator (subhanahu) covers it. From Ibn Abbas: the Lord of Might (wa jalla) covered it, and this is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters. Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and Ibrahim said: a locust of gold covers it. It is narrated from Mujahid that its branches changed into pearls, rubies and chrysolite (zabarjad).

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Salamah, who said: The angels asked the Lord, blessed and exalted, for permission to look at the Prophet (ﷺ), and He granted them permission, so the angels covered the lote-tree in order to look at him, peace and blessings be upon him. And in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of its leaves an angel standing, glorifying Allah, exalted is He." It was also said: a rafraf (green cloth or canopy) of green birds covers it. The ambiguity in all of this is of the same kind as what has preceded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ That is, the gaze of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn away from what it saw, *and it did not transgress*, but rather affirmed it with sound, certain affirmation. This is a confirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it. Or it means: he did not deviate from seeing the wonders he was commanded to see, nor did he go beyond them to what he was not commanded to see.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord.﴾ That is, by Allah, he saw the greatest of His signs and wonders, both of the realm of dominion (*mulk*) and of the realm of the unseen dominion (*malakut*), on the night of the Mi'raj (the Ascension). Here *al-kubra* (the greatest) is an adjective of a deleted noun, the object of *ra'a* (saw), which was placed in its position after its deletion. It was estimated in the plural to match the reality. It is also permissible that *al-kubra* is an adjective of the mentioned noun with the sense: "he saw *some* of the greatest signs." The first view was preferred because the context calls for glorification and emphasis, so it is fitting to state explicitly that what was seen was *the greatest signs*. The adjectival reading is also allowed, with *min* being redundant (*mazida*). You know that the redundancy of *min* in an affirmative sentence is not agreed upon as permissible.

Some reports specify what he saw, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said concerning the verse: "He saw a green *rafraf* (cushion/canopy) from Paradise that filled the horizon." And from Ibn Zayd: "He saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in the form in which he is." What should be held is that this is not to be taken as restrictive, as is clear, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) saw countless great signs on the night of the Mi'raj, which cannot be enumerated nor fully exhausted.

*Here there are other opinions concerning the verses, different from what preceded.* From al-Hasan: "the one of mighty power" (*shadid al-quwa*) is Allah, Most High, and the plural *al-quwa* (powers) is used for glorification. *Dhu mirra* (the Firm One) is interpreted by him as "possessor of wisdom" and similar expressions that are fitting as attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Abu Hayyan made the two pronouns in His saying, ﴿so He rose up﴾ and ﴿while He was on the highest horizon﴾, refer to Allah as well, Glorified is He. He said: this is in the sense of greatness, power and dominion. Perhaps al-Hasan makes the pronouns in His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, ﴿so He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾, refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as well. Likewise the object pronoun in His saying, Most High, ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾. He (may Allah have mercy on him) used to swear by Allah: "Muhammad (ﷺ) certainly saw his Lord." He interpreted the nearness of the Lord, Most High, to the Prophet (ﷺ) as the elevation of his status (ﷺ) with Him, Glorified is He, and His descent, Majestic and Exalted, as His drawing him with all his being toward the side of holiness. This drawing is called *al-fana' fi Allah* (annihilation in Allah, Most High) among the *mutaallihin* (those who speak of divinity; mystics). By His descent, Glorified is He, is meant a kind of His spiritual nearness, exalted is His majesty.

The position of the early generations (*al-salaf*) regarding such matters is to refer its knowledge to Allah, Most High, after negating resemblance (*tashbih*). It is also permissible that the pronouns in ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ refer, according to what was related from al-Hasan, to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning is: then the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) drew near to his Lord, Glorified is He, so there was from Him, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. The pronouns in *fa-awha* (so He revealed) and what follows refer to Allah, Most High. It was also said: ﴿to His servant﴾, and He did not say "to him," for the sake of magnification. The matter of the ambiguous verses (*mutashabih*) is known. Many have gone, concerning His saying, ﴿Taught him the One of mighty power﴾ up to His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾, to the view that it concerns the matter of revelation and its delivery from Jibril (peace be upon him), as you have heard above. And concerning His saying, Most High, ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾ and what follows, they went to the view that it concerns the matter of the ascent to the most holy presence, and His nearness, Glorified is He, to him (ﷺ), and his (peace be upon him) seeing Him, Majestic and Exalted. So the pronouns in *dana* (drew near), *tadalla* (descended), *kana* (was), *awha* (revealed), and likewise the object pronoun in *ra'a-hu* (saw him) refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is supported by the hadith of Anas in al-Bukhari, through the chain of Shurayk ibn Abdullah: "Then he ascended with him beyond that, to a degree known only to Allah, until he reached the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the Almighty, the Lord of Might, drew near and descended, until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer, and He revealed to him what He revealed: fifty prayers." The hadith is clear in what was mentioned.

The affirmers of the vision (*muthbitu al-ru'ya*) cited this, such as the scholar of the Ummah, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others. But A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, claimed otherwise. Muslim related from Masruq who said: "I was reclining with A'isha, and she said: O Abu A'isha, whoever says one of three things has greatly slandered Allah, Most High." I said: "What are they?" She said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly slandered Allah." He said: I was reclining, so I sat up and said: "O Mother of the Believers, give me time and do not hurry me. Did not Allah, Most High, say: ﴿And he certainly saw Him at the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23], ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾?" She said: "I was the first of this Ummah to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: No, it is only Jibril. I did not see him in his original form in which he was created except on these two occasions. I saw him descending from the sky, filling with the greatness of his creation the space between the sky and the earth." And the hadith continues.

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh through another chain, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq: "She said: I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and I said: O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord? He said: I only saw Jibril descending." It is not hidden that the answer of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) clearly indicates that the object pronoun in *ra'a-hu* does not refer back to Him, Most High, but to Jibril (peace be upon him). A'isha's view is that it negates that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw his Lord, Glorified is He, absolutely, and she takes as evidence His saying, Most High: ﴿No vision perceives Him, but He perceives vision﴾ [al-An'am: 103], and His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or send a messenger﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. This is evident in what al-Bukhari mentioned in his Sahih in the commentary of this surah. Some said: these verses only negate a vision that the verse we are discussing indicates, which is the one Masruq used as evidence.

The summary of what is related from her is the negation of the validity of using the mentioned verse as evidence for the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) vision of his Lord, Glorified is He, by clarifying that the referent of the pronoun in it is Jibril (peace be upon him), as indicated by the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) answer to her about it. The reading of his (peace and blessings be upon him) answer "No" in response to her as negating the specific vision, which is the one the verse is thought to indicate, returns to negating the indication. And the negation of the specific does not necessarily entail the negation of the general. The fair view is that the reports clearly indicate that she negates the vision absolutely, and she takes as evidence the two preceding verses. The affirmers of the vision have answered these two in what is mentioned in its proper place. Apparently Ibn Abbas did not speak of the vision except from hearing, and Ahmad related from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I saw my Lord." Muhammad al-Salihi al-Shami, a student of the Hafiz al-Suyuti, mentioned it in *al-Ayat al-Bayyinat* and authenticated it. Some combined the two statements of Ibn Abbas and A'isha by saying: A'isha's statement is to be understood as negating his seeing the Exalted in His light, which is the light described as one before which no sight can stand. Ibn Abbas's statement is to be understood as affirming the vision of the Exalted in His light, which does not blind the eyes, by the indication of his words in reply to Ikrima about the saying, Most High: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾: "Woe to you! That is when He manifests Himself with His light, which is His light." By this the reconciliation of the two hadiths of Abu Dharr becomes apparent. Muslim related through the chain of Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from Qatada, from Abdullah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Dharr who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Did you see your Lord? He said: 'A light, how could I see Him?'" [Note: the wording is as recorded in the commentary: "Nuraniyy aràhu" — "He is light; I see Him"]. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 17–18 (part 1 of 2):

﴿His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress.﴾ That is, the gaze of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn away from what it saw, *and it did not transgress*, but rather affirmed it with sound, certain affirmation. This is a confirmation of the matter and a negation of doubt concerning it. Or it means: he did not deviate from seeing the wonders he was commanded to see, nor did he go beyond them to what he was not commanded to see.

﴿Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord.﴾ That is, by Allah, he saw the greatest of His signs and wonders, both of the realm of dominion (*mulk*) and of the realm of the unseen dominion (*malakut*), on the night of the Mi'raj (the Ascension). Here *al-kubra* (the greatest) is an adjective of a deleted noun, the object of *ra'a* (saw), which was placed in its position after its deletion. It was estimated in the plural to match the reality. It is also permissible that *al-kubra* is an adjective of the mentioned noun with the sense: "he saw *some* of the greatest signs." The first view was preferred because the context calls for glorification and emphasis, so it is fitting to state explicitly that what was seen was *the greatest signs*. The adjectival reading is also allowed, with *min* being redundant (*mazida*). You know that the redundancy of *min* in an affirmative sentence is not agreed upon as permissible.

Some reports specify what he saw, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said concerning the verse: "He saw a green *rafraf* (cushion/canopy) from Paradise that filled the horizon." And from Ibn Zayd: "He saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in the form in which he is." What should be held is that this is not to be taken as restrictive, as is clear, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) saw countless great signs on the night of the Mi'raj, which cannot be enumerated nor fully exhausted.

*Here there are other opinions concerning the verses, different from what preceded.* From al-Hasan: "the one of mighty power" (*shadid al-quwa*) is Allah, Most High, and the plural *al-quwa* (powers) is used for glorification. *Dhu mirra* (the Firm One) is interpreted by him as "possessor of wisdom" and similar expressions that are fitting as attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Abu Hayyan made the two pronouns in His saying, ﴿so He rose up﴾ and ﴿while He was on the highest horizon﴾, refer to Allah as well, Glorified is He. He said: this is in the sense of greatness, power and dominion. Perhaps al-Hasan makes the pronouns in His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾, ﴿so He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾, refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as well. Likewise the object pronoun in His saying, Most High, ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾. He (may Allah have mercy on him) used to swear by Allah: "Muhammad (ﷺ) certainly saw his Lord." He interpreted the nearness of the Lord, Most High, to the Prophet (ﷺ) as the elevation of his status (ﷺ) with Him, Glorified is He, and His descent, Majestic and Exalted, as His drawing him with all his being toward the side of holiness. This drawing is called *al-fana' fi Allah* (annihilation in Allah, Most High) among the *mutaallihin* (those who speak of divinity; mystics). By His descent, Glorified is He, is meant a kind of His spiritual nearness, exalted is His majesty.

The position of the early generations (*al-salaf*) regarding such matters is to refer its knowledge to Allah, Most High, after negating resemblance (*tashbih*). It is also permissible that the pronouns in ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾, ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾ refer, according to what was related from al-Hasan, to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the meaning is: then the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) drew near to his Lord, Glorified is He, so there was from Him, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. The pronouns in *fa-awha* (so He revealed) and what follows refer to Allah, Most High. It was also said: ﴿to His servant﴾, and He did not say "to him," for the sake of magnification. The matter of the ambiguous verses (*mutashabih*) is known. Many have gone, concerning His saying, ﴿Taught him the One of mighty power﴾ up to His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿while he was on the highest horizon﴾, to the view that it concerns the matter of revelation and its delivery from Jibril (peace be upon him), as you have heard above. And concerning His saying, Most High, ﴿Then He drew near and descended﴾ and what follows, they went to the view that it concerns the matter of the ascent to the most holy presence, and His nearness, Glorified is He, to him (ﷺ), and his (peace be upon him) seeing Him, Majestic and Exalted. So the pronouns in *dana* (drew near), *tadalla* (descended), *kana* (was), *awha* (revealed), and likewise the object pronoun in *ra'a-hu* (saw him) refer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
