﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza,﴾ ﴿and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ These were idols that they worshipped. Al-Lat, as Qatada said, belonged to the tribe of Thaqif at al-Ta'if, and they recited:

Thaqif fled to their Lat,
returning defeated, losing.

Abu 'Ubayda and others said that it was at the Ka'ba. Ibn Zayd said that it was at Nakhla, near the market of 'Ukaz, and that Quraysh worshipped it. Ibn 'Atiyya preferred the view of Qatada. Abu Hayyan said: It is possible to reconcile these reports, by saying that what was named by this name were idols, and so he reported the location of each idol. As for its *ta'* (tā'), it is said to be original, being the *lam al-kalima* (the final radical of the root), like the *ba'* in *bab*. Its *alif* appears, as far as it seems, to be converted from a *ya'*, because the root *l-y-t* exists. But if the root *l-w-t* is attested, it may be that it was converted from a *waw*. It is also said that the *ta'* is the *ta' al-'iwad* (the compensatory tā'), and the original form was *lawya*, on the pattern *fi'la* from *lawa*, because they used to turn around it (*yalwuna 'alayhi*) and make retreat there for worship, or they would circle around it (*yaltawuna 'alayhi*), i.e., they would circuit it. So it was lightened by deleting the *ya'*, its *waw* was changed to an *alif*, and a *tā'* was put in place of the *ya'*, so it became like the *tā'* of *ukht* and *bint*. For this reason it is pausal with the *tā'*. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir, Abu Salih, Talha, Abu al-Jawza', Ya'qub, and, in one transmission, Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled *tā'*, as an *ism fa'il* (active participle) from *latta yaliltu*, meaning "he kneaded," when he kneads. It is said: there was a man who used to knead *sawiq* (parched-grain porridge) for the pilgrims on a stone. When he died, they worshipped that stone out of reverence for him, and named it by this name. It is also reported from Mujahid that it was on a rock at al-Ta'if, where he would prepare *hays* (a date-and-butter dish) and feed whoever passed by (*yamurru*) among the people. When he died, they worshipped it. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to knead *sawiq* on the stone, and no one drank from it without growing fat, so they worshipped it. Al-Fakihi reported from him that when he died, 'Amr ibn Luhayy said to them: "He has not died, but he has entered the rock," so they worshipped the rock and built a shrine over it. Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Juraij that he said: A man of Thaqif used to knead *sawiq* with oil, and when he died they made his grave an idol. People claimed that he was 'Amir ibn al-Zarib of 'Udwan. It has also been said otherwise.

(And al-'Uzza) belonged to Ghatafan. According to the well-known view, it was an acacia tree at Nakhla, as Qatada said. Its root is the feminine form of *al-a'azz* (the mightiest). Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Nakhla, where al-'Uzza was. Khalid came to it, and there were three acacias. He cut down the acacias and demolished the building that was over it. Then he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: 'Go back, for you have not done anything.' So Khalid went back. When the custodians (*sadana*) saw him, they fled, saying: 'O 'Uzza! O 'Uzza!' Khalid came to it and found a naked woman with disheveled hair, throwing dust on her head. He began to strike her with the sword until he killed her. Then he returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He, peace be upon him, said: 'That was al-'Uzza.'"

In another transmission: "He (ﷺ) sent Khalid to it, and he cut it down. A female devil came out of it, with disheveled hair, calling out her woe, placing her hand on her head. He struck her with the sword until he killed her, while saying:

O 'Uzza, [I reject] your disbelief; no glorifying of you!
Indeed I have seen that God has humiliated you.

He returned and informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, peace be upon him: 'That was al-'Uzza, and she will never be worshipped again.'"

Ibn Zayd said that al-'Uzza was at al-Ta'if, and Abu 'Ubayda said that it was at the Ka'ba. He supported this in the *Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's work) with the saying of Abu Sufyan in one of the battles to the Muslims: "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza." He mentioned in it that it was an idol, and it was pluralized in the same way as previously mentioned.

﴿And Manat﴾. It is said that she was a rock belonging to the tribes of Hudhayl and Khuza'ah. According to Ibn 'Abbas, she belonged to Thaqif, and according to Qatadah, she belonged to the Ansar at Qudayd. Abu 'Ubaydah said she was also in the Ka'bah. Abu Hayyan favored the view that all three were in it, saying: "Because the addressee in His words, ﴿Have you considered?﴾, is Quraysh." There is a discussion of this point. Manat is written with a final alif (maqsurah). It is said that her form is fa'alah, and she was named this because the blood of the sacrificial animals was poured out (tumna) at her, meaning shed. Ibn Kathir read it as Munat'ah with a long vowel and a hamzah, as in the verse of poetry, according to what is in al-Bahr:

"Has not Taym ibn 'Abd Manah come to us, despite the distance and the enmity between us, the son of Tamim?"

Its form is then maf'alah, and the alif is changed from a waw, as in maqalah. The hamzah is original, and the name is derived from al-nawʾ (the rising of a star, the seasonal rain), as if they used to seek rain through her, seeking blessing through her. The apparent reading is that ﴿the third, the other﴾ are two attributes of Manat. According to what is said, they are for emphasis, since her being the third and the other, different from what preceded her, is known and needs no explanation. Some of the eminent scholars said: ﴿the third﴾ is for emphasis, and "the other" is for dispraise, meaning she is later in rank and lowly in standing. Abu Hayyan objected that ākhar (another) and its feminine ukhrā were not established for dispraise or praise, but only indicate the meaning of "other." The truth is that this is considered with respect to the original meaning, and it does indicate dispraise of the two preceding ones as well. In al-Kashf it is said: "It is a term of dispraise indicating the lowliness of the two preceding ones in a certain respect, because ukhrā, the feminine of ākhar, requires sharing with the preceding one. So when it is used with the intention of being later in rank, acting on its original meaning (since the customary meaning cannot be applied, because the two preceding ones are not also third), it requires sharing, and so there is room for the sense of preference." It is as if it were said: "the other" in lateness. That is good. The reason given for dispraising Manat in this way is that the disbelievers used to claim that she was the greatest of the three, so God refuted them in this way.

The Imam said: ﴿the other﴾ is an attribute of dispraise, as if He, glory be to Him, had said: ﴿And Manat, the third﴾, the abased one. This is because al-Lat had the form of a human, ﴿al-'Uzza﴾ had the form of a plant, and ﴿Manat﴾ had the form of a rock. The human is nobler than the plant, and the plant is nobler than the inanimate, so the inanimate is later. Manat is inanimate, so she is at the lowest of ranks. You know that this does not hold under all opinions. It is also said that ﴿the other﴾ is an attribute of al-'Uzza, because she is the second of al-Lat, and the second is called "the other." It was placed later to match the endings of the verses. Al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaddal said:

"There is inversion and displacement in the speech, and the intended meaning is: 'and al-'Uzza, the other, and Manat, the third.' By my life, this is nothing."

The address is to the worshippers of these mentioned idols. Although they worshipped them, they used to say that the angels, peace be upon them, and these false objects of worship were the daughters of God. Exalted is God far above that, with great exaltation. So it was said to them as rebuke and reproach: ﴿Have you considered?﴾, and so on. The interrogative particle is for denial, and the fa' is for directing it toward the arrangement of the sight (ru'yah) upon what has been mentioned of the affairs of God, which are utterly contrary to it. The verb here is, according to many, cognitive (ʿilmiyyah). Its second object, according to what some have chosen, is omitted, indicated by the situation. So the meaning is: Is it after what you have heard of the signs of the perfect greatness of God, mighty and majestic, in His dominion, His kingdom, His splendor, His might, the perfection of His power, and the execution of His command, that you have seen these idols, with their utmost worthlessness, as daughters of God, glory be to Him and exalted?

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ is a rebuke built upon that earlier rebuke. Its basis is the preference of their own side over His Majesty, since they assigned to Him the females and chose for themselves the males. The basis of the first (rebuke) is this very attribution. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Have you considered these idols, despite their lowliness and abasement, as partners of Allah, glorified is He, given His greatness that has preceded?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "Tell me about your gods: do they possess any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might has been described in the preceding verses?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "Do you suppose that these idols you worship benefit you?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "Have you considered these idols: if you worship them they do not benefit you, and if you abandon them they do not harm you?" It is not hidden that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is it for you﴾ and so on does not fit with what precedes it under all these opinions the way it fits with the earlier opinion. It has also been said that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Is it for you﴾ and so on is in the position of the second object of "seeing" (ru'yah), and its being free of a pronoun referring back to the first object is because the original sense is: "Tell me: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, is it for you the male and for Him they are the females?" That is, those idols. So the feminine ﴿al-unthā﴾ was placed in their position for the sake of observing the verse-endings (fawasil) and for establishing the basis of the rebuke. Yet this, despite its artificiality, requires that the rebuke be limited to preferring their own lowly, abased side over the side of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, without addressing the rebuke over attributing offspring to Him, glorified is He. In al-Kashshaf, the excellence of the composition is that, after He had depicted the matter of revelation in a complete depiction and established that what he hears is revelation without any doubt, because he saw the one who brought it and knew him with the fullest knowledge, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12], meaning: "Will you argue with him after these clarifications over what is seen of the clear signs, since he is upon a clear proof from his Lord, glorified is He, a guide who is guided? And how could there remain any room for dispute, when he has seen Him in another descent?!"
Page 57

And he knew Him with the fullest knowledge. Then it was said: ﴿He had indeed seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ and so on, as an alert that what is counted among them is also a negation of misguidance and error and an affirmation of insight and guidance.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is a conjunction upon "will you dispute with him" (tumarunahu). The interrogative particle was introduced to add emphasis to the denial, and the fa' (then) is because saying such things is a consequence of obstinacy, stubbornness and not listening to the call of truth. The meaning is: "After this clarification, will you persist in what you are upon of disputation, so that you see al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat as offspring of His, exalted is He?" Then He reduced them to baseness, and His saying ﴿Is it for you﴾ and so on filled the place of the second object, adding denial. On this basis, "Have you considered?" (afara'aytum) is not in the sense of a question, though it may be in its sense, on the meaning of ﴿Will you dispute with him?﴾, so: "Tell me: is it for you the male and for Him the female?" The saying is implied, that is: "Then say to them: Tell me," and the meaning is: "It is such-and-such," in mockery and as an alert that this is the result of their disputing, and that whoever holds this belief is in the error beyond which there is no error. It is not far from such people to attribute to the guided, guiding ones what they are in of deficiency. End. What he mentioned first is better, and it is not far from what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 22:

﴿Tilka﴾ (That) is a reference to the division implied by the interrogative sentence, ﴿idhan qisma-tun ḍīzā﴾ (This would be an unjust division). That is, unfair, in that you have assigned to Him, glory be to Him, what you yourselves disdain. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada explained ḍīzā this way. Similar in meaning is Sufyan's view that it means "deficient" (manqūṣa), Ibn Zayd's that it means "contrary" (mukhālifa), Mujahid's and Muqatil's that it means "crooked" (ʿawjāʾ), and al-Hasan's that it means "not balanced" (ghayr muʿtadila). Apparently it is an adjective. Its yāʾ has been disputed: some say it is converted from a wāw, and others say it is original. Its pattern is fuʿlā with a ḍamma on the fāʾ, like ḥubla and unthā, and then the fāʾ was kasra so that the yāʾ would be preserved, as was done in bīḍ, the plural of abyaḍ, whose pattern is fuʿl with a ḍamma on the fāʾ, like ḥumr, and then the fāʾ was kasra for the reason mentioned. Such a thing is common. Its pattern was not taken to be fiʿlā with a kasra from the outset, following the view of Sibawayh that fiʿlā with a kasra does not occur among the Arabs in adjectives. However, some have made it so, relying on the occurrence of such forms. Thaʿlab recorded mishya ḥīkā (a gait), rajul kīṣā (a man), and others recorded imra’a ʿizhā (a woman) and imra’a siʿlā (a woman). This was refuted on the grounds that these are rare forms, and that analogy with the frequent and regular forms of the category is preferable. It could also be said that ḥīkā and kīṣā are subject to what was said about ḍīzā, and the occurrence of ʿizhā and siʿlā is disputed, since the known forms are ʿizhāh and siʿlāh. It is also permitted that ḍīzā be fiʿlā with a kasra from the outset, as a verbal noun like dhikrā, and used as an adjective for emphasis. The occurrence of this kind of adjective among verbal nouns, as mentioned, and among fixed nouns like difalā and shiʿrā, and among plurals like ḥijlā, is common. Ibn Kathir read ḍiʾzā with a hamza, as a verbal noun used as an adjective. It is also permitted that it be an adjective with a ḍamma, treated as a weak-letter form because it reverts to that. Ibn Zayd read ḍayzā with a fatha on the ḍād and a yāʾ, as in daʿwā or sakrā. It is also said ḍuʾzā with a wāw and a hamza and a ḍamma on the fāʾ. Al-Kisa'i recorded ḍaʾaza yaḍʾazu ḍaʾzan with a hamza, and al-Akhfash recited:

Though you turn away from her, she will hunt you, and if you are absent, your arrow is struck and your nose is humbled.

The more common form is ḍaza without a hamza, in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

The Banu Asad were unjust in their judgment, when they made the head like the tail.

Ibn ʿAbbas also recited this line in explaining his interpretation mentioned above.

Page 58

﴿They are nothing but names﴾: the pronoun refers to the idols, meaning the idols, considered in terms of the divinity you claim for them, are ﴿nothing but names﴾, pure names, with not the least trace of the meaning of divinity in them. God's words ﴿that you have named﴾ are a qualifier of the names, and the pronoun in it refers to the names, not to the idols. The meaning is "that you have made them names." Naming (*tasmiyah*) is a relation between the name and the named. When it is considered in relation to the name, its meaning is making it a name for the named. When it is considered in relation to the named, its meaning is making it named by the name. The first meaning was chosen here, without reference to the named, to establish that those idols which they call gods are bare names with no named referents at all, as in God's words, glorified is He: ﴿You worship besides Him only names﴾ [Yusuf: 40], and so on. This does not mean that there are named referents which do not deserve the name. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the three names mentioned, since they applied them to those idols because they believed that the idols deserve devotion, honour, and offerings made to draw near to them. This has been objected to: even if we grant that the three names indicate that those pure meanings are present in the idols, denying them of the idols adds no further benefit. Rather, the benefit lies in denying divinity of them, as is their well-known claim concerning all idols, in a demonstrative manner. The negation of the attribute is by way of a stronger inference, that is, they are not anything at all except names devoid of named referents, which you have devised, ﴿you and your fathers﴾, according to vain desires, ﴿God has sent down no authority for them﴾, no proof on which they may rely. ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned of naming and acting upon it, they follow only conjecture, ﴿only the supposition﴾ that what they hold is true, a vain supposition. Thus *al-zann* (conjecture) here means supposition, and its use for this meaning has become common. It is understood from the words of al-Raghib that supposition is one type of conjecture. ﴿And what the souls desire﴾, that is, what their commanding souls, which incite to evil, long for. Here *ma* is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted. The *al-* in *al-anfus* (the souls) is for familiarity, or it is a substitute for the genitive complement. It has also been permitted that *ma* is a verbal-noun (*masdariyyah*) particle, and likewise it has been permitted that *al-* is generic, meaning that the soul, insofar as it is soul, only desires what is less than best, because it is inclined to love of pleasures, and only the intellect leads it to a good outcome. The *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, here a shift to the third person, which signals that the enumeration of their ugly deeds called for turning away from them and relating their crimes to others) in *yattabi'una* (they follow). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read *tattabi'una* (you follow) with the second person. ﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *yattabi'una*, establishing the falsehood of what they hold, namely following conjecture and desire. By *al-huda* (the guidance) is meant the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, or the Mighty Qur'an, either in the sense of "the guiding one," or it is made into guidance as an intensive. That is, they follow nothing but that. The circumstance, namely that there has certainly come to them from their Lord, may He be exalted, is such that they should not abandon it or follow other than the path of truth. The summary of this is: they follow that in a state which contradicts it. It has also been permitted that the sentence be a parenthetical clause, which also emphasises the falsehood of that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 24:

﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ (Am) is a disjunctive particle (munqati'a), with an implied (muqaddara) "bal" (rather/nay). It serves to shift from explaining that what they are upon is supported by nothing except their illusions and the desires of their souls, to explaining that this is something that brings no benefit at all. The hamza is for denial and negation, meaning: rather, there is not for man everything that he wishes and that his soul desires. Its implication has been said to be: the removal of the universal affirmation, and its return is to a particular negative proposition (salbah juz'iyyah). Some of them alluded to this when they said: the intended meaning is the negation that the disbelievers should have what they hoped for, namely the intercession of the gods and attaining the good reward with Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection, and what they desired of the revelation of the Qur'an being sent down to a great man from one of the two cities, and the like. It is understood from the words of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) that the intended meaning is the universal negation, and the meaning is: nothing of what man wishes is owned by him, exclusively his, to dispose of according to his will. This includes the negation that the disbelievers should have what was mentioned. Man is not specific to them, as has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 25–26:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the Hereafter and the First (life)﴾, is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the negation of that. The exclusivity of the dominion over all the affairs of the Hereafter and the First (life) to Him, Exalted is He, necessitates that no affair whatsoever belongs to the human being. Rather, whatever Allah, Exalted is He, wills for him comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. The Hereafter is mentioned first out of concern to refute what is more important to them among their hopes, namely their success in it. For this reason He followed that with His saying, Exalted is He:

[Page 59]

﴿And how many an angel in the heavens, their intercession will not avail at all﴾. Despairing them of what they hoped for from the intercession of the angels, peace be upon them, necessarily entails despairing them of the intercession of the idols by way of greater priority. ("How many", kam) is an informative (khabariyyah) particle indicating multiplicity. Its position is nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is the negative clause. The pronoun in "their intercession" is plural, while "the dominion" is singular, by consideration of meaning. That is: and many of the angels, their intercession with Allah, Exalted is He, will not avail anything at all, at any time, ﴿except after Allah gives permission﴾ to them for intercession.

﴿for whomever He wills﴾ that they intercede on his behalf, ﴿and is pleased with﴾, and sees him, glory be to Him, as worthy of intercession from among the People of Monotheism and faith. As for those other than them from among the People of disbelief and transgression, they are far removed from the permission of Allah, Exalted is He. It is also reported from Him that it is "a thousand thousand stations." It is also permissible that the meaning is: except after Allah gives permission to whomever He wills among the angels to intercede, and sees him, Mighty and Majestic is He, as worthy of it. Whichever of these is the case, the meaning is that if the condition of the angels regarding intercession is as mentioned, then what do they presume about the condition of the idols? It has been said that the statement belongs to the type of the poet's words: "On a broad road whose landmarks cannot be followed." Its sum is: there is no intercession for them, nor any avail, without Allah, glory be to Him, giving permission, and so on. It has also been said that it comes as a hypothetical supposition (fard), and so it does not contradict His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255].

Zayd ibn Ali read "shafa'atuhu" (his intercession), with the singular for both the intercession and the pronoun. Ibn Muqsim read "shafa'atuhum" (their intercessions), with both in the plural. This is also the choice of the author of al-Kamil, Abu al-Qasim al-Hudhali. The word "intercession" is singular in the recitation of the majority, and Abu Hayyan said: because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and because if all of them interceded for a single person, their intercession would not avail him anything at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 27:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ — and in what it contains of punishment — for what they engage in of disbelief and sins. ﴿surely name the angels﴾ — who are free of all attributes of deficiency absolutely — ﴿with the name of females.﴾ For they used to say, "The angels are the daughters of Allah, glorified and exalted is He above what they say." The word "al-malā'ikah" (the angels) here carries the sense of encompassing each individual (istighrāq al-mufrad), so the meaning is: they name each one of the angels with the name of a female, i.e., they call each one of them a daughter, because when they say this, they have made each one of them a daughter. The statement is in the pattern of "kasānā al-amīru ḥullatan" (the governor clothed us, a robe), i.e., he clothed each one of us with a robe. The singular form (al-unthā) is used because there is no ambiguity. For this reason it did not say "tasmiyata al-inath" (the naming of females), so there is no need to interpret "al-unthā" as "al-inath" (females) or to take the intended meaning as "the female group." What was mentioned first has been said to be based on the view that "tasmiyata al-unthā" in the noble verse is not an accusative of resemblance (naṣban ʿalā al-tashbīh); otherwise there is no need for it either. In linking the naming to not believing in the Hereafter there is an indication that this act is so grievous and monstrous, and so liable to bring punishment in the Hereafter, that none would dare to do it except one who does not believe in it at all.

And His saying, ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject (fā'il) of *yusammūna* ("they name"). The pronoun *bihi* ("of it") refers to the naming mentioned, and it is in the masculine on that account. Alternatively, it refers to the saying, meaning: they name them females, while the reality is that they have no knowledge at all of what they say. Ubayy read *bihā* ("of it," feminine), meaning the naming, or else referring to the angels. ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾, meaning: in this matter they follow nothing but baseless delusion (*tawahhum*). ﴿And indeed conjecture﴾: that is, conjecture as a genus, as the use of the explicit noun in the place of a pronoun (*al-iẓhār fī mawqi' al-iḍmār*) hints. It has been said that the explicit noun is used so that the sentence stands on its own like a proverb.

﴿Avails nothing against the truth﴾, from *al-ighnā'* ("to avail"). The truth (*al-ḥaqq*), which is the reality of a thing and what it is, is grasped in a way that counts only when it comes from certainty and not from conjecture or delusion. Therefore conjecture is not relied upon in matters of the real cognitions, namely the doctrinal matters (*al-maṭālib al-i'tiqādiyyah*) in which firm conviction is required, even if it is not based on proof. It is relied upon only in practical matters (*al-'amaliyyāt*) and in what leads to them.

Some have interpreted "the truth" as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, based on His saying: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾ [al-Ḥajj 22:6, 22:62; Luqmān 31:30]. Whoever does not regard *taqlīd* (blind adherence to authority) as valid in doctrinal matters uses this verse as evidence, though this is open to discussion. The Ẓāhirīs (the Ẓāhiriyyah, a literalist school) hold that *taqlīd* is invalid absolutely, and they refute *qiyās* (analogical reasoning) and reject it completely, as is thoroughly treated in the works of *uṣūl* (legal theory).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ayyūb, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said:

"Beware of this opinion (*ra'y*) in religion, for the opinion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was correct only because Allah was showing it to him, whereas ours is merely contrivance and conjecture."

﴿And indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾ is also one of their proofs for invalidating *qiyās*. Al-Āmidī, in *al-Iḥkām*, reported something similar from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Suspect opinion in matters of religion, for opinion is from us merely contrivance and conjecture," and then ﴿And indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾. He answered this by saying that its utmost implication is only that there is a possibility of error in it, and there is nothing in it that proves its invalidity. He also said that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿indeed conjecture﴾ and so on is the use of conjecture in places where certainty is required, and that the intent is not to invalidate conjecture, as is shown by the validity of acting on the apparent meanings of the Book and the Sunnah. The same may be said regarding the words of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him. He mentioned a number of reports which those who invalidate *qiyās* cited in support of their claim, and he refuted all of them. Whoever wishes that should refer to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 29:

﴿So turn away from those who turn away from Our remembrance﴾ That is, from them. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed in the position of their pronoun in order to make the attribution of the negative qualities contained in its clause (silah) the means of describing them, and to make those qualities the cause (ta'lil) of the ruling. That is: turn away from those who have turned away from Our remembrance, meaning the Qur'an the Mighty, which conveys the true knowledge, which contains the clarification of the correct beliefs, which encompasses the sciences of the earlier and the later people, and which reminds of the Hereafter and of the matters in it that are desired and those from which one flees. By turning away from it is meant abandoning acting upon what is in it and not caring for it. It is also said: the "remembrance" means the Messenger (ﷺ), and turning away from him means abandoning acting upon what he brought. It is also said: it means faith. It is also said: it is on its apparent meaning, and turning away from it is a metaphor (kinayah) for heedlessness of Him, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And he desires nothing but the life of this world﴾, being content with it, confining his outlook to it, striving earnestly for what sets it right, like al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. The command mentioned means a prohibition against overdoing eagerness for their guidance, as if it were said: Do not overdo your eagerness for the guidance of those who have turned away from Our remembrance and have immersed themselves in this world, such that it is the furthest extent of their aspiration and the utmost of their striving.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That﴾ refers to the matter of the worldly life that is understood from the discourse; for this reason the demonstrative noun was mentioned. It was also said: it means what led them to what they are in of turning away and restricting their aspiration to the worldly life. It was also said: "that" refers to the supposition which they follow. It was also said: it refers to their making the angels daughters of Allah, glorified is He. Both of these opinions are as you see. ﴿Their knowledge extends no further﴾, meaning: the limit of their knowledge is that they have no knowledge beyond it. This is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad, interjected statement) that establishes the meaning of what precedes it, namely the restriction of their aspiration to the worldly life.

By "knowledge" is meant mere perception (idrak) that is organized around a corrupt supposition. The pronoun in ﴿their limit﴾ refers back to "man" (liman), and it is in the plural in consideration of its meaning, just as its singular form was used in consideration of its wording. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to turn away. The repetition of His saying, the Exalted, "He is most knowing" serves to increase the affirmation and to signal the complete difference between the two known groups. By ﴿who strays﴾ is meant one who persists in error and never returns to guidance at all; by ﴿who is guided﴾ is meant one whose nature is to be guided in general. That is: He, exalted is His majesty, is the one most thorough in knowledge of the one who will never desist from error, and of the one who accepts guidance in general, and not anyone else, glorified is He. So do not wear yourself out in calling them, and do not be excessive in your eagerness for them, for they are of the first category.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 31:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning: to Him belongs that in the most complete manner, that is, creation and dominion, with no one else having any share in it at all, neither independently nor jointly, Exalted and Majestic is He. It implies a verb to which it is connected.
Page 61

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That He may recompense those who did evil for what they did﴾, meaning: He created what is in them so that He may recompense the misguided with the punishment for what they did of misguidance, which He expressed by "evil" as a clarification of their state; or with the like of what they did; or because of what they did, with the bāʾ being connected to "recompense" by an implied noun (muḍāf), or for causation without any implied element. ﴿And that He may recompense those who did good﴾, meaning: those who were guided, ﴿with the best﴾, meaning: with the best reward, which is Paradise; or with what is better than their deeds; or because of their good deeds. This is a complement to what precedes, because when He, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to turn away, He negated the assumption that they would be left unaccounted for. In changing from the pronoun "your Lord" to the all-encompassing Name there is an indication of increased power, and that the speech is directed at warning those who turn away, and that the ordering of this great dominion is for this wisdom: there must be a misguided one and a guided one, and each must receive what he deserves. In it is also that he, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, receives the best reward for his conveying, while they receive evil, that is, as recompense for their denial. The verb of recompense is repeated to show the full care given to it and to draw attention to the difference between the two recompenses.

It is also permitted that the meaning of ﴿So turn away﴾ etc. is: do not confront them with their conduct, and entrust them to your Lord; indeed He knows best about you and about them, so He recompenses each with what he deserves. The departure from the two pronouns in "those who went astray" and "those who were guided", and making His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿That He may recompense﴾ dependent on what is indicated by His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord, He is most knowing﴾ etc., according to this, is not hidden: that is, He distinguished the one who went astray from the one who was guided and preserved their states, ﴿that He may recompense﴾ etc. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, is a parenthetical clause affirming that they will certainly be recompensed and not left neglected, as if it were said: He, glorified is He, knows best about them, and they are under His dominion and power. It was also permitted, on this meaning, that ﴿That He may recompense﴾ be connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, as mentioned before, to emphasize the matter of the warning, meaning: He knows best about them, and He arranged this dominion for recompense. Some scholars preferred this meaning on the two grounds mentioned above. It was also permitted for the clause ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "knows best", whether it is in the sense of "knowing" or not. And for ﴿That He may recompense﴾ to be connected to "went astray" and "was guided", with the lām being for consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), meaning: He, Exalted is He, ﴿knows best who has gone astray﴾ so that his affair will end with Allah, Exalted is He, recompensing him for his deeds, ﴿and who has been guided﴾ so that his affair will end with His recompensing him with the best. Its remoteness is not hidden, and even more remote by many stages is its connection to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Their intercession will avail them nothing﴾, as Makki mentioned. Zayd ibn ʿAli recited "linajziya" and "najziya" with the nūn in both.

﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the gross indecencies﴾. [The phrase] ﴿alladhina yajtanibuna﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the second relative noun (al-mawsul al-thani). The imperfect form in its relative clause indicates the renewal and continuance of avoiding them. It may also be an explanatory apposition (bayan), a qualifier (na't), an accusative of praise (mansub 'ala al-madh), or a nominative whose predicate is omitted (marfu' 'ala annahu khabar mahdhuf).

(﴿al-ithm﴾) is the act that hinders one from reward, namely sin (dhanb). Its major sins (kaba'ir) are those whose punishment is great. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿kabira al-ithm﴾ (in the singular), treating it as a generic noun (li-iradat al-jins), or referring to shirk.

﴿wa-al-fawahish﴾ are those of the major sins whose ugliness is greatest. Their conjunction with what precedes is the conjunction of the specific with the general. It was also said that "the indecencies" (al-fawahish) and "the major sins" (al-kaba'ir) are synonyms.

﴿illa al-lamam﴾: lamam is what is small of sins. Its root meaning is that whose quantity is little, and from it comes lummat al-sha'r (a small lock of hair), since it is less than the full wafra (a longer lock). Abu Sa'id al-Khudri explained it as a glance, a touch, and a kiss, and this is an example (min bab al-tamthil). It was also said that its meaning is approaching something without committing it, from almamtu bi-kadha (I came near to such a thing and approached it without engaging in it). On this is the saying of al-Rummani: it is the intention to commit a sin and the inner speech of the soul without actually doing it. The saying of Ibn al-Musayyab: it is what occurs to the heart. From Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd: it is what they committed of shirk and sins in the Jahiliyya before Islam. The verse was revealed in response to the saying of the disbelievers to the Muslims: "You used to do our deeds yesterday." It is thus like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you combine two sisters [in marriage], except what has already passed﴾ [an-Nisa' 23], according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). It was also said: it is absolute sin.

[Page 62]

In a narration from Ibn 'Abbas, it is what a person commits momentarily of sins and then repents. The one who magnifies [the verse] by interpreting it as minor sins, the exception is disconnected (istithna' munqati'). It was also said: there is no exception in it at all. And ﴿illa﴾ is a qualifier (sifa) meaning "other than" (bi-ma'na ghayr). This is either because the noun annexed to a definite noun with the generic al (the annexed phrase "major sins of sin," i.e. kaba'ir al-ithm) is treated as indefinite, or because ghayr and illa, which share this meaning, may both become definite by annexation, as in ﴿other than those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatiha 7]. Some have objected to this, that the condition for ﴿illa﴾ to be a qualifier is that it follows an indefinite plural that is not restricted, and this condition is not met here. It was answered that this is the view of Ibn al-Hajib, but Sibawayh holds that it may be a qualifier together with being an exception, so he does not require that condition, and most later scholars followed him. Yet its being a qualifier here is contrary to the apparent sense, and there is no need to resort to it.

The verse, according to most scholars, is evidence that sins are of two kinds: major and minor. A group of imams denied this division and said: all sins are major. Among them are Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, Imam al-Haramayn in al-Irshad, Taqi al-Din al-Subki, and Ibn al-Qushayri in al-Murshid. Indeed, Ibn Furak related it from the Ash'aris and chose it in his own tafsir, saying: all of God's disobediences are, in our view, major, and only some of them are called minor and major in relation to one another. He reported the division as held by the Mu'tazila and said it is not correct. Qadi 'Abd al-Wahhab said: it is not possible to say of a sin that it is minor except in the sense that it becomes minor by avoiding the major sins. This agrees with what al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, though it is disconnected (munqati'), that the major sins were mentioned in his presence and he said: everything God has forbidden is a major sin. In another narration: every matter in which God is disobeyed is a major sin.

The majority hold the division. It was said: there is no disagreement in meaning; the disagreement is only over the naming and the application of the term, since all agree that among sins are those that undermine uprightness ('adala) and those that do not. The first group avoided the naming, disliking to call a disobedience "minor," because when viewed in relation to the overwhelming greatness of God, every disobedience is great. The majority did not consider this, because it is known, and they divided sins according to what is mentioned in the apparent texts of the verses and hadiths. For this reason al-Ghazali said: it is not fitting to deny the distinction between major and minor sins, since we have learned it from the sources of the Shari'a.

Then, those who uphold the distinction differed about the definition of a major sin. It was said: it is that for which its doer is threatened by a specific severe warning in the text of the Book or the Sunna. This is the expression of many jurists. It was also said: every sin that requires a fixed penalty (hadd), and this was the view of al-Baghawi and others. The first is more in keeping with what they mentioned in detailing the major sins, for they counted backbiting, tale-bearing, disobedience to parents, and others among them, for which there is no hadd. So the first is more correct than the second, although al-Rafi'i said: they lean toward preferring it. It may be objected to the first also that they counted among the major sins what has no specific severe warning attached.

It was also said: it is every act the Book explicitly forbade, or for which a hadd is required in its category, and abandoning an obligatory duty that must be performed immediately, and lying in testimony, in narration, and in oath. Al-Harawi and Shurayh added: every statement that contradicts the general consensus. It was also said: every offence that indicates the perpetrator's little concern for religion and weakness of piety. This is what is related from Imam al-Haramayn, and a group preferred it for its precision. It was objected that by its outward sense it includes the minor sin of baseness, whereas the Imam, as al-Adhra'i said, defined by it only those sins that nullify uprightness, which include the major ones but are not limited to them. Yet it is more comprehensive than the first two definitions.

It was also said: it is what requires a hadd or is subject to a threat (wa'id), as mentioned by al-Mawardi in his fatawa. It was also said: every act forbidden in itself, prohibited for a reason inherent in itself. If its doing combines two or more aspects of prohibition, it is a fahisha (gross indecency). Thus fornication is a major sin, and adultery with a neighbour's wife is a gross indecency. A minor sin is the commission of something whose rank is lower than the rank of what is explicitly stated, or committing it in a way less than what is explicitly stated. If one commits it in a way that combines two or more aspects of prohibition, it becomes a major sin. So kissing, touching, and thigh-contact are minor sins, but with a neighbour's wife they become major. Ibn al-Rif'a and others transmitted this from al-Qadi Husayn, from al-Hulaymi.

[Page 63]

It was also said: it is every act the Book explicitly forbids, that is, in the wording of prohibition (lafz al-tahrim). These are four things: eating carrion, the flesh of swine, the property of an orphan, and fleeing from the battlefield. This was rejected on the ground that it does not limit the category. It was also said: it is every sin accompanied by a hadd, a threat, or a curse in a text of the Book or Sunna; or known to have a corruption similar to what is accompanied by these, or greater; or indicative of the perpetrator's disregard for his religion in a way that diminishes the major sins explicitly mentioned. An example is one who kills a person he believed to be protected, then it becomes clear that the victim deserved to be killed, or one who has intercourse with a woman supposing she was an adulteress, only to find she is his wife or his slave-woman. This is the view of Shaykh al-Islam al-Bulqini (al-Barizi), who said it is the correct position. Others said other than this. Al-Wahidi relied on the view that there is no limit that delimits them. He said: the correct view is that major sins have no definition by which the servants can know them, for otherwise people would rush into minor sins and regard them as lawful. Rather God concealed this from them so that they would strive to avoid what is forbidden, hoping that the major sins would be avoided. A parallel to this is the concealment of the Greatest Name, the Middle Prayer, the Night of Decree, and the hour of answered supplication.

The scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said: all the definitions mentioned were intended only as approximations, otherwise they are not comprehensive definitions. How is it possible to fix what there is no hope of fixing? Others sought to define them by counting. From Ibn 'Abbas: they are what God mentioned at the beginning of Surat an-Nisa' up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden﴾ [an-Nisa' 31].

It was also said: they are seven, and this is narrated from 'Ali, may God honour his face, and from 'Ata' and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. It is argued from what is in the two Sahihs: "Avoid the seven destructive sins: associating partners with God, sorcery, killing a soul which God has forbidden except by right, consuming the property of an orphan, consuming usury, turning away on the day of battle, and accusing chaste, unaware, believing women." It was also said: fifteen; it was said: fourteen; it was said: four. From Ibn Mas'ud: three. In another narration: ten. Shaykh al-Islam al-'Ala'i said: what is explicitly stated in the hadiths as major is twenty-five. Ibn Hajar objected to him by adding more to that. Abu Talib al-Makki said: they are seventeen. Four are of the heart: shirk, persistence in disobedience, despair, and feeling secure from God's plan. Four are of the tongue: slander, false testimony, sorcery (and it is every speech that alters a person or one of his limbs), and the oath of perjury (al-yamin al-ghamus), which is the oath by which one nullifies a right or establishes a falsehood. Three are of the belly: consuming the property of an orphan wrongfully, consuming usury, and drinking any intoxicant. Two are of the private parts: fornication and sodomy. Two are of the hand: murder and theft. One is of the foot: fleeing from the battlefield. One is of the whole body: disobedience to parents. And there is in this what there is.

Al-Tabarani related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man said to him: "How many are the major sins, are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven; however, there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence." Many scholars have composed works on this, and in the book az-Zawajir by the scholar Ibn Hajar there is what suffices, so let it be consulted. And God is the Granter of success, and we seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance.

﴿Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness﴾, in that He forgives minor sins to those who avoid the major sins. So the clause is a justification (ta'lil) for the exception of al-lamam, and an indication that its exclusion from the ruling of accountability is not because it is free of sin in itself, but because of the vastness of divine forgiveness. It is also permissible that the meaning is that He, glorified is He, may forgive to whomever He wills among the believers whatever sins He wills, minor or major. Perhaps the reason for following the threat to the evildoers and the promise to the good-doers with this is so that the one guilty of a major sin does not despair of His mercy, exalted is He, and does not imagine that punishment is obligatory upon him, mighty and majestic is He. Some claimed it is permissible that the relative noun (al-mawsul) be the subject and this sentence its predicate, with an omitted resumptive pronoun, meaning ﴿of vast forgiveness﴾ toward them. This is nothing, as is not hidden.

﴿He knows you best﴾, that is, He knows your circumstances better than anyone, ﴿when He produced you﴾ within the production of your father Adam, peace be upon him,

[Page 64]

﴿from the earth﴾ in a general production, as its realization has been discussed earlier. It was also said: their production from the earth is in view of the fact that the semen from which they are formed comes from foods whose origin is the earth. Whichever is the case, ﴿idh﴾ ("when") is an adverbial complement (zarf) governed by ﴿a'lamu﴾ ("knows best"), and it remains in its original sense of specifying time.

Makki said: it means "knower" ('alim), since the Exalted's knowledge is related to their states at that time, and He has no partner in that. This was challenged on the ground that the knowledge of those whom God Most High has informed, from among the angels, may also relate to it. It was also said that "idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, the sense being: "Remember when He produced you" (﴿إذْ أنْشَأكُمْ﴾), and this, as you see, is [a weak view]. ﴿وإذْ أنْتُمْ أجِنَّةٌ﴾ ("and when you were embryos") — the time of your being embryos ﴿فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهاتِكُمْ﴾ ("in the bellies of your mothers") in various successive stages, is not hidden from Him, glorified is He. It is a state of your states and a deed of your deeds, among which is the minor lapse (al-lamam), whose consequence would have befallen you had it not been for the vast forgiveness. Thus the sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it. The mention of ("in the bellies of your mothers") although the embryo was not in the belly [itself] is to indicate the stages, as we have pointed out. It was also said: it is to emphasize the importance of knowledge, since the belly of the mother is in the utmost darkness. The "fa" (so) in His saying ﴿فَلا تُزَكُّوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ ("so do not justify yourselves") is for the consequence: the prohibition of self-justification follows from what was said earlier, namely that the non-punishment for the minor lapse is not because it is not of the category of sins, but purely because of His forgiveness, while He knows full well that it proceeds from you. That is: since the matter is so, do not praise yourselves for being completely free from disobedience, or for the purity of your deeds and the abundance of good in them; rather, thank God Most High for His bounty and His forgiveness, majestic is His glory. ﴿هُوَ أعْلَمُ بِمَنِ اتَّقى﴾ ("He knows best who is God-fearing") — [He knows] who has avoided sins entirely. This is a resumptive clause confirming the prohibition, and it indicates that among them are those who avoid them completely, as stated in al-Irshad. It was also said: [the one who] avoided shirk; and it was said: [the one who] avoided some of the sins. The verse, it is said, was revealed concerning a group of believers who used to perform good deeds and then say, "Our prayer, our fasting, and our pilgrimage"; this is blameworthy and forbidden when it is done by way of self-admiration or showing off. But when it is not so, there is no harm in it, and its doer is not counted among those who justify themselves. For this reason it has been said: "Joy in obedience is itself obedience, and mentioning it is gratitude." There is no difference in self-justification between its being by expression and its being by allusion, and among it is counted naming someone with such names as Barrah (pious). Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Sa'd narrated from Zaynab bint Abi Salamah that she was named Barrah, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not justify yourselves; God knows best who is righteous among you. Name her Zaynab." Likewise, the Prophet (ﷺ) changed the name Barrah bint Jahsh to this. Changing such a name is recommended. Likewise, whatever name some people use that would bring about a negative omen in something, such as Barakah and Yasar; the prohibition against naming with it is for reasons of disapproval (tanzih). The saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as narrated by Jabir: "If I live, God willing, I will forbid my community from naming [their children] Nafi', Aflah and Barakah," is interpreted, as al-Nawawi said, to mean that "forbid" here is a prohibition of prohibition (nahy tahrim). The apparent view is that the disapproval of a name that suggests self-justification is specific to cases where the suggestion is strong, as when the name, before being transferred, clearly indicates the naming and is used for it. So there is no disapproval in naming with a name that suggests praise when it is not like that, such as Sa'id and Hasan. "Umar, may God be pleased with him, had a daughter called 'Asiyah, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) named her Jamilah," so it is said. The matter still does not lack a need for investigation, so let it be examined. It was also said: the meaning of "do not justify yourselves" is: do not let some of you justify others; what is intended is the prohibition of praise for show or for worldly gain, or praise in a definitive manner. As for justification for establishing rights and the like, it is permissible. Some scholars held that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews.

Al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews, whenever a young child of theirs died, said: 'He is a saint (siddiq).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'The Jews have lied. No soul that God creates in its mother's belly is without His knowing its happiness or its misery.'" Then God, glorified is He, revealed at that point ﴿هُوَ أعْلَمُ بِكُمْ﴾ ("He knows you best"), and the verse [continues].

[Page 65]

﴿Have you considered the one who turns away﴾, that is, from following the truth and remaining steadfast upon it, ﴿and gives little﴾, that is, a little of something, or a small giving, ﴿and withholds﴾, that is, he ceased giving. It comes from their saying "he dug and *akda*" (ahkada, "he struck hard ground") when he reached a *kudya*, meaning a hard rock in the earth, so digging became impossible for him.

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had heard the recitation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, sat with him, and was admonished by him, so he drew near to Islam, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ hoped for him. Then a man among the polytheists rebuked him and said: "Will you abandon the religion of your fathers? Return to your religion and remain upon it, and I will bear for you everything you fear in the Hereafter, but on condition that you give me such-and-such amount of wealth." Al-Walid agreed to this, turned back from what he had intended of Islam, and went far astray. He gave some of the wealth to that man, then withheld the rest and became stingy.

Al-Dahhak said: It is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. He gave five she-camels to a poor man from among the Muhajirun until he apostatized from his religion, and he guaranteed to him that he would bear his sin for his return (to disbelief).

Al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who used to agree with the Prophet ﷺ in some matters.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: It concerns Abu Jahl, who said: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands noble character."

The first view is the most well-known and the most suitable to what follows it, His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ and so on to the end of the verse. As for what is in al-Kashshaf, that it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, who used to give his wealth in charity, and Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh said to him: "It is likely that nothing will remain for you," and Uthman said: "Indeed I have sins and faults, and by what I do I seek the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and hope for His pardon." Abdullah said: "Give me your she-camel with its saddle, and I will bear all your sins for you." So he gave it to him, had him witness it, and withheld from giving. This is false, as Ibn Atiyya said, and it has no basis, and Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, is free of such a thing.

Nor does the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, detract from this: "Whoever establishes a bad practice in Islam, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." For that is the burden of misguiding, which is his own burden, not the burden of another.

Allah's words, ﴿And that man will not have except what he strove for﴾, explain that a person is not rewarded for the deeds of others, following the explanation that he is not held accountable for the sin of others. ("That" [wa-anna]) is like its preceding counterpart. "Ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and it has been permitted that it be a relative pronoun, meaning: he has nothing except his striving, or except that for which he strove and which he did. This raises a difficulty, since authentic reports have come concerning the benefit of charity given on behalf of the dead. Among them is what Muslim, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i transmitted from A'ishah: "A man said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'My mother died suddenly, and I think that if she had been able to speak, she would have given charity. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'My sister vowed to perform Hajj, and she has died.' The Prophet (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: 'If she had a debt, would you have paid it?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then the right of Allah is more deserving of being fulfilled.'"

It has been answered that when someone else intends that act on behalf of the deceased, he becomes like an agent (wakil) standing in his place in the eyes of the Law, so it is as though the effort is his own. This is not possible except through an extended figurative usage (umum al-majaz), or through combining the literal and figurative meanings according to those who permit it.

It has also been answered that the striving of another benefits him only when it is based on his own striving, namely faith, so it is as though it were his striving. What indicates that it is based on this is what Ahmad transmitted from Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather: that al-As ibn Wa'il vowed in the pre-Islamic period to sacrifice one hundred camels (badanah), and that his son Hisham sacrificed fifty, which was roughly his share; and that Amr asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about that. He said: "As for your father, if he had affirmed Tawhid (the Oneness of Allah), and you had fasted and given charity on his behalf, that would have benefited him."

This answer has been given to what is said: that the multiplication of reward mentioned in the verses also contradicts restricting benefit to one's own striving alone. You know what is problematic in this answer.

One of the eminent verifiers said: it has been reported in the Book and the Sunnah what is decisive concerning the attainment of benefit from the deeds of others, and this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, so it is restricted to what the doer does not bestow.

The governor of Khurasan, Abdullah ibn Tahir, asked al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl about this verse together with Allah's words, ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. He said: "By justice, he has only what he strove for; and by grace, he has what Allah wills." Abdullah then kissed al-Husayn's head.

Ikrimah said: this ruling applied to the people of Abraham and Moses, peace be upon them both. As for this Ummah, a person benefits from the striving of others. This is indicated by the hadith of Sa'd ibn Ubadah: "Will it be of benefit to my mother if I perform voluntary acts on her behalf?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes."

Al-Rabi' said: "man" here refers to the disbeliever; as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf.

From Ibn Abbas it is reported that the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by Allah's words, ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith — We shall join with them their descendants﴾ [al-Tur: 21]. He transmitted from him what suggests this, Abu Dawud and al-Nahhas both in the book on abrogating verses (al-nasikh), and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh.

Abu Hayyan criticized the narration of abrogation, saying that it is not sound, because the verse is a report (khabar) that does not contain an obligation, and there is no abrogation in reports.

What might be suggested as an answer, that Allah informed in the law of Moses and Abraham, peace be upon them both, that reward would not be given to anyone other than the doer, and then He granted it to those after them among the people of our law, returns to restricting the reports rather than to abrogation, since its reality is that the meaning is intended and then, after that, its intention is lifted. This is a specification of the intention with respect to the people of the laws. So understand this.

It has also been said: the lam (in "li-l-insan") means "upon" ('ala), meaning: there is nothing upon man except his striving. This is far from its apparent meaning and also from the context of the verse, for it is an admonition to the one who turned away, gave little and held back.

What I incline to is the statement of al-Husayn, and similar is the statement of Ibn Atiyyah. He said: "The clarification, in my view, regarding this verse is that the core of the meaning is the lam in His words, glory be to Him: (li-l-insan). So when you determine what it is that a person may rightly say is 'mine,' you will find nothing except his striving. As for mercy through intercession, or the care of a righteous father or a righteous son, or the multiplication of good deeds, or something similar, that does not belong to the person, and he may not say 'this is mine' except by way of metaphorical extension and attachment to what is truly his." End of quotation.

From the totality of what has preceded, it is known that the Mu'tazilah's (the rationalist school) use of the verse to argue that if a servant makes the reward of any deed he does belong to another, it does not take effect and his bestowal is void, is invalid. Likewise, al-Shafi'i's use of it to argue that the reward of recitation does not reach the dead (which is also the position of Imam Malik) is not conclusive. Rather, Imam Ibn al-Humam said: Malik and al-Shafi'i do not hold that purely bodily acts of worship such as prayer and recitation reach the dead, but rather other acts such as charity and Hajj do.

In al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar, may Allah have mercy on him, it is said: the well-known position of the school of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, and of a group of scholars, is that they do not reach. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and a group of scholars, and some of al-Shafi'i's own followers, held that they do reach. So the preferred practice is that the reciter, after finishing, says: "O Allah, convey the reward of what I have recited to so-and-so." It seems that if he says this or similar, such as "I have gifted the reward of what I recited to so-and-so," in his heart, that suffices. It has been reported from some of them that the intention of acting on another's behalf must be made at the start of the recitation, though there is some doubt about this.

Then it seems that this applies when the recitation is not for a wage. But if it is for a wage, as most people do today, giving the memorizers of the Qur'an payment to recite for their dead, and they recite for that payment, then its reward does not reach, since there is no reward for it to reach, because taking payment for reciting the Qur'an is forbidden, though it is not forbidden for teaching it. This was verified by the final of the verifying jurists, Shaykh Muhammad al-Amin ibn Abidin al-Dimashqi, may Allah have mercy on him.

In al-Hidayah, in the book of Hajj, concerning performing Hajj on behalf of another, there is an absolute statement that a person's making his deed belong to another is valid, even if it is prayer or fasting, according to the people of the Sunnah and the community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jama'ah). In it there is what you have known from what has passed just now.

Al-Khafaji said: this needs clarification, and its clarification is that the place of disagreement concerns bodily worship: can it be substituted, so that the obligation falls from the one who is responsible by another's doing it, whether with his permission or not, during his life or after his death? This has occurred in the Hajj, as is found in the sound hadiths. As for fasting, it is not so. As for what has come in the hadith, "Whoever dies owing fasting, his guardian shall fast on his behalf," and similarly other acts of worship, al-Tahawi said: this was in the early period of Islam and was then abrogated. The discussion is not about ransom (fidyah) and feeding people, for that is a substitute. Likewise, gifting the reward, whether in its very form or in its like, is a supplication, and its acceptance is by Allah's grace, glory be to Him, like charity on behalf of another. Understand this." End of quotation. So do not be heedless.

﴿And that He is the Lord of al-Shi'ra.﴾ Al-Shi'ra is al-'Abur (the Crosser), with a fatha on the 'ayn (unpointed ع), a fatha on the ba' (single dot), and an unpointed ra' after the waw. It is also called al-Shi'ra al-Ghumaysa', with a dammed ghayn (dotted غ), a fathed mim, then a ya' (with two dots beneath), an unpointed sad, and a long vowel (madd). The first is in al-Jawza' (Orion). It was called al-'Abur because it crossed the Milky Way (al-Majarra) and met Suhayl (Canopus). It was also because, when it rises, it appears as though it is about to cross. It is also called Kalb al-Jabbar (the Dog of al-Jabbar), because it follows al-Jawza', which is named al-Jabbar, just as a dog follows the hunter or the prey. The second is in the outstretched Dhira' al-Asad (the Forearm of the Lion). It was called al-Ghumaysa' because it wept over its separation from Suhayl, so its eye became inflamed. Al-Ghamas is the liquid that flows from the rheum, a white filth that gathers in the corner of the eye. This is based on the Arabs' belief that the two are sisters of Suhayl. In the Qamus (the lexicon), among their tales, it is said that al-Shi'ra al-'Abur crossed the Milky Way and was therefore named 'Abur, and the other wept after her until her eye became inflamed. It is also called al-Ghamus. It was also said: they claimed that Suhayl and al-Shi'ra were a married couple. Suhayl descended and became a Yemeni, and al-Shi'ra followed him, crossing the Milky Way, and was therefore named al-'Abur. The Ghumaysa' remained, and was named thus because she is less bright than the first. All of this is among their false imaginings that have no reality. The one that comes to mind when the name is used without a descriptor is al-'Abur, because it is larger in body and brighter, and it is the one that was worshipped besides Allah, the Glorified, in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). Al-Suddi said: Himyar and Khuza'ah worshipped it. Others said: the first to worship it was Abu Kabsha, a man from Khuza'ah, or he was their chief.

They used to claim that every trait in a person passes to him from one of his ancestors, so they would say: "The vein of so-and-so has pulled him toward him," and "the vein of the maternal uncle is a puller." Some have mentioned that he was one of the Prophet's (ﷺ) forefathers on his mother's side. They used to claim that every trait in a person passes to him from one of his ancestors, so they would say: "The vein of so-and-so has pulled him toward him," and "the vein of the maternal uncle is a puller." It was also said that Abu Kabsha is the kunya (teknonym) of Wahb ibn 'Abd Manaf, the Prophet's (ﷺ) grandfather on his mother's side. Their saying this to him (ﷺ) would, according to the apparent meaning of the Qamus, refer to a resemblance in character, not in opposition. It was also said that Abu Kabsha is the kunya of the husband of Halima al-Sa'diyya, his (ﷺ) wet-nurse, or of the paternal uncle of her son. Because she was worshipped besides Him, the Mighty and Majestic, she was singled out for mention, so that this would be a rebuke to them by making the one who is lord into a servant. For greater emphasis on this, the statement was framed as a nominal sentence, as the sublime composition expresses.

Among the Arabs there were those who revered it, believed in its influence on the world, and claimed that it cuts across the sky horizontally, while the other stars cut across it lengthwise. They spoke about hidden matters at its rising. So in the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﹙and that He is the Lord of al-Shi'ra﹚, there is an indication of the denial of its influence.

﴿And that He destroyed the first 'Ad﴾, i.e., the ancient ones, because they were the first nation to be destroyed after the people of Nuh, as Ibn Zayd and the majority said. Al-Tabari said: it was described as "the first" because among the tribes there is another 'Ad. That was a tribe in Mecca along with the 'Amaliq, who were the Banu Luqaym ibn Hizal. Al-Mubarrad said: the other 'Ad is Thamud. It was also said: they are the tyrants. It was also said: the first 'Ad are the children of 'Ad ibn Iram ibn 'Awf ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and the other 'Ad are from the children of the first 'Ad. In al-Kashshaf (the Kashshaf), "the first" refers to the people of Hud, and "the other" is Iram. And Allah knows best.

It is also permitted that "the first" refers to the earlier nobles. A group read ﻋﺎﺩ ﺍﻟُﻮﻟﻰ, dropping the hamza and transferring its damma to the lam before it. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read ﻋﺎﺩﺍﻟُّﻮﻟﻰ, assimilating the tanwin into the lam to which the vowel of the dropped hamza was transferred. Al-Mazini and al-Mubarrad found fault with this reading. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 51–52:

﴿And Thamud﴾: it is coordinated (ʿatf) with ʿAdan (ʿAd), and it cannot be the object (maf'ul) of "li-ubqa" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so He left none remaining﴾, because the negating "ma" has the initial position in the sentence, and the particle "fa" is, as it is said, also preventive, so the object (maʿmul) of what follows it may not precede it. It is also said that it is an object of a suppressed "li-ahlaka" (He destroyed), but there is no need for it. ʿAsim and Hamzah read "Thamud" without tanwin (nunation), and they stop without an alif, while the rest read it with tanwin and stop with an alif. The apparent meaning is that the complement of "abqa" refers to both ʿAd and Thamud together, meaning: "so He left none of them remaining," i.e., He seized them for their sins. It is also said: meaning, He left none of them remaining, and what is intended is that He left none of their disbelievers remaining. ﴿And the people of Nuh﴾ is also coordinated with ʿAdan. ﴿From before﴾ means from before the destruction of ʿAd and Thamud. The priority was explicitly stated because Nuh, peace be upon him, is the second Adam, and his people were the first of the tyrants and those destroyed. ﴿Indeed they were the most wrongdoing and the most transgressing﴾, meaning, of the two groups, in that they used to harm him and beat him until he could hardly move. A man among them would take his son by the hand and walk with him to him, warning him against him and saying: "O my son, my father walked me to this man when I was like you that day, so beware lest you believe him," and the elder would die in disbelief and the young would grow up on his father's instruction. They were not affected by his call, though he had called them for a thousand years minus fifty years. It is also said: the pronoun in "indeed they" refers to all those mentioned before, ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Nuh, meaning that they were more wrongdoing than the Quraysh and more transgressing than them, and in this there is a consolation for the Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, which is not hidden. The "hum" may be an emphasis (taʾkid) for the object pronoun, and it may be a separator (fasl), because it falls between a definite noun and an elative (afʿal al-tafdil). The second term of comparison was omitted together with what occurs as the predicate of "kana," because it runs in the manner of the predicate of the subject (mubtada'), and its omission is eloquent in that case, so likewise in the predicate of "kana."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 53:

﴿And the overturned cities﴾ are the towns of the people of Lut (ﷺ)... 

Let me be precise and complete in the translation below.

﴿And the overturned [cities]﴾ are the towns of the people of Lut (peace be upon him). They were so named because they were overturned with their inhabitants, i.e., they were turned upside down with them. From this comes the word ifk (falsehood), because it is the inversion of truth. It is also permissible that by al-Mu'tafikah is meant everything whose dwellings have been overturned and whose places have been obliterated.

Al-Hasan read "al-Mu'tafikat" in the plural. ﴿Ahwa﴾ means He brought them down to the earth after having lifted them on the wing of Jibril (peace be upon him) up to the sky. Al-Mubarrad said: He made them fall (tahwi).

It is apparent that ahwa governs al-Mu'tafikah, and the governing verb has been placed last because it is a fasilah (rhyme-closing word). It is also permissible that al-Mu'tafikah is in coordination (ma'tuf) with what precedes it, and "ahwa" together with its subject forms a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), with qad implied, or without it, clarifying the manner of their destruction.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 54–55:**

﴿Then there covered them that which covered them.﴾ In it is an expression of the terror (*tahwil*, the emphasis on dread) of the punishment, and a generalization of what befell them from it, because the relative pronoun *al-mawsul* (*ma*) is among the forms that denote generality. The doubling in *ghashsha* (the *tashdid* on the *shin*) may be for transitivity (*ta'diyah*), in which case *ma* is the second object and the agent is His pronoun, may He be exalted. It may also be for intensification and emphasis (*takthir wa-mubalaghah*), in which case *ma* is the subject.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ *Tatamara* means to doubt. The form *tafa'ul* here is free of the sense of plurality in agent and object, for the sake of intensifying the action. It has been said that the verb *tamari* is singular in form, given the plurality of its object, which is *al-ala'* (the blessings) about which one disputes. The address has been said to be to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as a kind of stirring (*ilhab*) and an indirect address meant for others. It has also been said to be to mankind in general, and this is more apparent. The interrogative is for denial (*inkar*).

*Al-ala'* is a plural meaning blessings (*ni'am*). What is meant by it is what was enumerated in the preceding verses. The whole is named thus, even though some of it consists of punishments (*niqam*), because punishments contain lessons (*'ibar*) and admonitions for those who take heed, and benefit for the prophets and the believers. Hence they are blessings in this respect too. It has also been said that the use of *al-ala'* is by way of predominance (*taghlib*), though this has been objected to on the ground that the context does not suit it.

Ya'qub and Ibn Muhaysin read *rabbika tatammara* (رَبِّكَ تَّمارى) with a doubled *ta'* (تاءٍ مُشَدَّدَةٍ).
