This is a commentary on surah 53, verse 56:

﴿This is a warner from the warners of old.﴾ The reference (al-ishara) is to the Qur'an. Abu Malik said: it refers to the report about the earlier nations, or the reference is to the Messenger (ﷺ). The word nadhir (warner) comes both as a verbal noun (masdar) and as a descriptive adjective (wasf), and nudhur is its plural in general use. Each of the two meanings is possible here. The description nudhur is in the plural as a qualifier of "the earlier" (al-ula) on the basis of interpreting it as a group (firqa) or a company (jama'a), and it was chosen over the alternatives in observance of the rhyme (fasila). Whatever the case, the meaning of ﴿This is a warner from﴾ the category (jins) of ﴿the warners of old﴾ is clear.

In al-Kashshaf it is stated that His words, exalted is He, ﴿This is a warner﴾ and so on, are a summation (fadhlaka) of the discourse, either of what was enumerated of the contents of the scrolls (suhuf), or of the whole discourse from the opening of the surah. So reflect on this, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verses 59–61:

﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾, that is, the Qur'an, in denial, ﴿and laugh, mocking,﴾ although it is the furthest thing from that, ﴿and do not weep,﴾ out of grief over what you have neglected concerning it, and out of fear that there will befall you what befell the nations mentioned, ﴿while you are sāmidūn,﴾ that is, heedless, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas in reply to Nafi' ibn al-Azraq. He recited to support this the verse of Hudhaylah bint Bakr, weeping for the people of 'Ad:

"Would that 'Ad had accepted the truth and not shown denial."

It was said: "Rise and look at them, *** then leave off your sumud."

In another report, he (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about sumud, and he said: it is *al-barṭamah*, which is raising the head in arrogance. That is, while you raise your heads in arrogance. Its interpretation as *al-barṭamah* was also narrated from Mujahid. Al-Raghib said: *al-sāmid* is the heedless one who raises his head, from *samada al-ba'īr* in his walk, when he raised his head. Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-sumud* is singing in the language of Himyar, who say: "O girl, *usmidī* for us," that is, sing for us. Something similar was narrated from 'Ikrimah. 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and a group, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: it is singing in the Yemeni manner, and when they heard the Qur'an they would sing to distract themselves from it. It was also said: they did this so as to distract people from listening to it. The nominal clause, on all of these interpretations, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of *lā tabkūn*, and its content is a qualification of the negation; the denial is directed at the negation of weeping and at the existence of sumud. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-sumud* is stillness and humility, as in the verse:

"The calamities of time have struck the women of the family of Sa'd *** with a measure, and they have fallen into sumud because of it.
So their black hair turned white, *** and their white faces turned black."

On this view, the clause is also a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of *tabkūn*, except that its content is a qualification of the negated, and the denial falls on the negation of both weeping and sumud together, so do not overlook this.

In the codex of Ubayy and in that of 'Abd Allah, *tadhakūn* appears without a *wāw*. Al-Hasan read *tu'jibūn, tuḍḥikūn*, without a *wāw*, with the two *tā's* vowelled with a *ḍammah* and the *jīm* and *ḥā'* with a *kasrah*. The verse has been cited, as in Aḥkām al-Qur'ān, as evidence for the recommendation of weeping when hearing and reciting the Qur'an. Al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the verse *﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾* was revealed, the companions of the Suffah wept until their tears ran down their cheeks. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard their sobbing, he wept with them, and we wept at his weeping. Then he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'The one who weeps out of fear of Allah the Exalted will not enter the Fire, and the one who persists in his disobedience will not enter Paradise. Even if you did not sin, Allah the Exalted would bring a people who sin, then they would seek forgiveness, and He would forgive them.'"

Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad and others narrated from Salih Abu al-Khalil, who said: "When this verse was revealed, *﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse? And you laugh and do not weep﴾*, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not laugh after that except to smile." The wording of 'Abd ibn Humayd is: "The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was not seen laughing or even smiling until he departed from the world." In this is the closing of the door of laughter for the reciters of the Qur'an, even if it were not mockery, and we seek refuge in Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 53, verse 62:

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾. The fa' (فاء) here indicates the sequence of the command, or its consequence, based on what has been established of the falsehood of responding to the Qur'an with wonder and laughter, and of the correctness of responding to it with what befits it, and it indicates the greatness of its status. That is: and since the matter is as such, then prostrate to Allah, the Exalted, who sent it down, and worship Him, Majestic is His majesty. This is a verse of prostration according to the majority of the scholars ('ulama'), and the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated at it.

Al-Shaykhan, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The first surah in which a prostration was revealed is ﴿al-Najm﴾, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and all the people prostrated except a man..." — the hadith.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer, and he recited al-Najm, and he prostrated with us, and he prolonged the prostration." And likewise 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Sabra, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab led us in the Fajr prayer, and he recited in the first rak'ah Surat Yusuf, then he recited in the second rak'ah Surat al-Najm and prostrated, then he stood and recited Idha zulzilat, then he bowed." Malik does not hold prostration here, and he cited as evidence what Ahmad, al-Shaykhan, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani and others narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "I recited al-Najm in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate in it." It is answered that abandoning it only negates the obligation of the prostration, and it is not agreed upon; and according to the one who holds it, it is to be performed with latitude (al-tarakhi) in such matters, according to the preferred view. The hadith contains nothing that indicates its complete negation, so it is possible that he (ﷺ) prostrated afterwards, and likewise Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him. Yes, delay is disliked as a matter of recommendation (tanzih), and perhaps he did it to demonstrate permissibility, or for an excuse we are not aware of. As for what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas as his saying: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not prostrate in any of the mufassal since he moved to Medina," it is negating and weak. Likewise his saying in what he also narrated from him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to prostrate in al-Najm in Mecca, and when he emigrated to Medina, he abandoned it," since abandoning it only negates, as you have heard, the obligation. And Allah knows best.
